title: A Virtual Member of a Community of Practice for the Society of Petroleum Engineers: From Prototype to Deployment
summary: We describe the evolution of a virtual assistant, called ATHENA, designed to support the capture, retrieval, and dissemination of knowledge for members of a Community of Practice (CoP) related to the Oil and Gas sector. An evaluation of a first prototype involving 75 professionals from the Society of Petroleum Engineering (SPE) showed that ATHENA dramatically improved both their productivity and performance equality on a set of realistic well-planning tasks compare to their use of a state-of-the-art RAG baseline system. However, the evaluation also identified areas for improvement. This paper describes technical advances to our first prototype in the areas of multi-document retrieval, support for answer validation, and more focused proactive dissemination. Evaluation results show that this enhanced version of ATHENA provides better support for completing knowledge-intensive tasks related to well planning than does a state-of-the-art baseline. ATHENA has been integrated into the SPE Research Portal and is being deployed for use by the society's membership.

AI.tldr: ATHENA is an improved virtual assistant for oil and gas Communities of Practice that significantly outperforms a strong RAG baseline on knowledge-intensive well-planning tasks and is now being deployed via the SPE Research Portal.
AI.motivation: Professionals in the oil and gas sector, particularly in Communities of Practice like the Society of Petroleum Engineering, must handle complex, knowledge-intensive tasks such as well planning that require efficient capture, retrieval, and sharing of specialized knowledge. Existing state-of-the-art RAG systems do not provide sufficient productivity, performance equality across users, or proactive knowledge dissemination. The authors aim to build and refine a virtual assistant that more effectively supports these real-world workflows and closes these gaps.
AI.method: The authors first built a virtual assistant, ATHENA, tailored to the oil and gas CoP, and evaluated it with 75 SPE professionals on realistic well-planning tasks against a state-of-the-art RAG baseline. Based on observed shortcomings, they introduced technical improvements in three key areas: (1) multi-document retrieval to better aggregate and reason over information from multiple sources, (2) mechanisms for answer validation to increase reliability and user trust, and (3) more focused proactive dissemination of relevant information. They then re-evaluated the enhanced ATHENA on knowledge-intensive well-planning tasks, again comparing it to the baseline system.
AI.result: The initial prototype of ATHENA significantly improved user productivity and reduced performance disparities among SPE professionals compared with a strong RAG baseline, but also exposed limitations in retrieval, answer validation, and information push. After implementing multi-document retrieval, answer validation support, and more targeted proactive dissemination, the enhanced ATHENA demonstrated further performance gains and superior support for completing knowledge-intensive well-planning tasks compared to the state-of-the-art baseline.
AI.conclusion: ATHENA, a virtual assistant designed for Communities of Practice in the oil and gas domain, can substantially outperform generic state-of-the-art RAG systems on complex, domain-specific tasks when enhanced with multi-document retrieval, answer validation, and focused proactive dissemination. The system’s integration into the SPE Research Portal and ongoing deployment indicate that such tailored assistants are practical, effective, and ready for real-world adoption by professional communities.

title: Transformer Models for Text Summarization: A Comparative Study of BART, BERT, and RoBERTa
summary: Text summarization refers to the task of condensing a document into a shorter version while preserving its key information. Automatic text summarization (ATS), driven by advancements in natural language processing (NLP), has developed rapidly in recent years. ATS methods are commonly categorized by input type (such as single-document or multi-document summarization) and by output type (extractive, abstractive, and hybrid). This article presents a focused review of modern summarization techniques with an emphasis on transformer based models and large language models (LLMs), specifically BERT, RoBERTa and BART. It examines their architectures, pretraining strategies, and their suitability for extractive and abstractive summarization tasks.

AI.tldr: A review of modern automatic text summarization with a focus on transformer-based and large language models like BERT, RoBERTa, and BART, analyzing how their architectures and pretraining make them suitable for extractive and abstractive summarization.
AI.motivation: To clarify and synthesize how recent transformer-based and large language models are used for automatic text summarization, and to compare their capabilities for different summarization types.
AI.method: Literature review and conceptual comparison of summarization methods, especially transformer-based models (BERT, RoBERTa, BART) and their architectures, pretraining setups, and applications to extractive vs. abstractive summarization.
AI.result: The paper characterizes how BERT, RoBERTa, and BART are architected and pretrained, and evaluates or describes their respective strengths and limitations for extractive and abstractive summarization tasks.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based LLMs, particularly BERT, RoBERTa, and BART, play a central role in modern automatic text summarization, with different models being better suited to extractive or abstractive summarization depending on their architecture and pretraining.

title: Automatic bioinformatic software named entity recognition from literature
summary: Bioinformatics software and databases are essential components of modern life science research, yet their mentions in the scientific literature are often inconsistent and difficult to systematically identify at scale. The lack of a comprehensive and up-to-date catalog of bioinformatics resources hinders efforts toward automated biomedical knowledge extraction and streamlined data analysis. Here we present SNAIL, a hybrid named entity recognition framework designed to automatically identify bioinformatics software and database (SW/DB) names from biomedical texts. SNAIL integrates complementary lexical and semantic modeling strategies. The lexical component captures orthographic patterns and contextual cues characteristic of SW/DB names, while the semantic component leverages contextual embeddings generated by transformer-based language models such as SciBERT, combined with an explicit token-masking strategy to enhance entity-focused representations. A large training corpus was constructed automatically through a hybrid pipeline that integrates citation-hinted extraction with large language model-assisted distillation. Evaluation on two independent benchmark datasets and real-world research articles demonstrates that SNAIL substantially outperforms existing approaches, including domain-specific methods such as bioNerDS2 and general-purpose large language models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude. Applying SNAIL to large-scale literature analysis further reveals distinct journal-level preferences across bioinformatics subfields. These results demonstrate that SNAIL provides an accurate and scalable solution for identifying bioinformatics resources in scientific texts and enables systematic meta-analysis of tool usage and research trends.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SNAIL, a hybrid NER framework that accurately and scalably detects bioinformatics software and database names in biomedical literature.
AI.motivation: Mentions of bioinformatics software and databases in scientific articles are inconsistent and hard to detect automatically, and there is no comprehensive, up‑to‑date catalog of such resources. This gap limits automated knowledge extraction, tracking of tool usage, and streamlined data analysis across the life sciences.
AI.method: SNAIL is a hybrid named entity recognition framework that combines: (1) a lexical component capturing orthographic patterns and local contextual cues typical of software/database names; and (2) a semantic component based on transformer language models (e.g., SciBERT) with a token-masking strategy to focus representations on candidate entities. The authors also construct a large training corpus automatically using a hybrid pipeline that couples citation-based hints with large language model–assisted distillation, then evaluate SNAIL on benchmark datasets and real-world articles.
AI.result: On two independent benchmark datasets and real research articles, SNAIL significantly outperforms both specialized domain NER tools (e.g., bioNerDS2) and general-purpose large language models (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Claude) at identifying bioinformatics software/database names. Large-scale application of SNAIL to the literature uncovers different journal-level preferences in tool usage across bioinformatics subfields.
AI.conclusion: SNAIL offers an accurate, scalable solution for recognizing bioinformatics software and database names in biomedical texts. Its hybrid lexical–semantic design and automatically built training corpus enable superior performance over existing methods and make it suitable for constructing comprehensive catalogs of bioinformatics resources, supporting systematic meta-analyses of tool usage and research trends.

title: Asymmetric Attention Heads: Structured Head-Wise Context Allocation for Transformer Attention
summary: Standard multi-head attention (MHA) gives every head the same full causal context span, although heads can serve different contextual roles. Some heads may rely mainly on nearby lexical or syntactic context, while others may depend on longer-range relations such as entity interactions, discourse links, or state changes. We present Asymmetric Attention Heads (AAH), a head-wise context- allocation framework that treats context length as an explicit per-head or per-group allocation variable. AAH groups heads using feature-derived statistics, organizes these groups hierarchically, and assigns causal local windows while preserving the standard flat MHA output interface. In 4096- token seed-0 experiments, several AAH-style local-allocation variants achieve lower validation loss than pure full attention. Short-budget ablations show that stable local allocation and head-window assignment structure matter, while fixed/local controls can be competitive with adaptive hierarchy. We interpret AAH as a structured head-wise context-allocation mechanism for quality and analysis, with Attention Coverage Ratio (ACR) reported as a selected-window routing diagnostic

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Asymmetric Attention Heads (AAH), a framework that allocates different context window lengths to different attention heads, improving language model performance and offering better interpretability metrics such as Attention Coverage Ratio (ACR).
AI.motivation: In standard multi-head attention, every head has access to the same full causal context, even though different heads specialize in different types of dependencies (e.g., local syntax vs. long-range discourse). This uniform treatment can be inefficient and obscures how context is actually used by each head. The authors are motivated to design a structured, head-wise mechanism that explicitly controls and analyzes how much context each head receives, aiming to improve efficiency, performance, and interpretability.
AI.method: They introduce Asymmetric Attention Heads (AAH), where context length is an explicit allocation variable per head or per head-group. Heads are grouped based on feature-derived statistics and organized in a hierarchy. Each group is then assigned a causal local context window size, effectively giving some heads shorter local windows and others longer ranges, while keeping the external MHA interface unchanged. They compare several AAH-style local allocation schemes against standard full attention and various baselines, including short-context budget settings and fixed/local controls. They also introduce Attention Coverage Ratio (ACR) as a diagnostic to assess how selected windows route attention across tokens.
AI.result: In experiments with 4096-token context and a specific seed (seed-0), multiple AAH-style local context allocation strategies achieve lower validation loss than standard full attention. Ablation studies on short-budget settings reveal that having a stable, structured allocation of local windows to heads is important; naive or unstable allocations underperform. Fixed/local window baselines, however, can be competitive with more complex adaptive hierarchical strategies, indicating that much of the gain comes from principled head-wise window assignment rather than sophisticated adaptivity alone.
AI.conclusion: AAH is presented as a structured approach to per-head context allocation in multi-head attention that can improve model quality while enabling more interpretable analysis of attention-head roles. By assigning different context window sizes to different heads or head groups and measuring Attention Coverage Ratio (ACR), the method offers both performance benefits and a tool for understanding how attention resources are distributed across context. The framework suggests that explicit, stable local allocation and head-window structure are key design dimensions for attention-based language models.

title: Active Inference as Context Acquisition for AI Agents
summary: Interactive AI agents must acquire the right context as efficiently as possible. When a user omits a constraint, preference, file, or task variable, an agent can proceed with a default assumption or spend tokens on a clarifying question, retrieval call, tool call, or prompt trial. We formulate this tradeoff as active inference for context acquisition. An inner inference step updates beliefs over a latent task state, and an outer decision selects the next context action, task action, or stop action to minimize expected free energy under cost. In deterministic settings, the epistemic term reduces to expected information gain, optionally normalized by token cost. We instantiate the framework in Optimal Question Asking (OQA), with exact posteriors and a dynamic programming oracle, and benchmark frontier language models on binary and multiway categorical tasks from 25 to 300 candidates. We also study clarification before generation and automated prompt optimization under token budgets. The formulation is model-agnostic and views active inference as a design principle for the context-acquisition layer of AI agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a decision-theoretic framework for when an AI agent should ask questions, retrieve context, or proceed with assumptions, modeling this as active inference that trades off information gain against token cost.
AI.motivation: Interactive AI agents often lack full task context—users omit constraints, preferences, files, or variables—so the agent must decide whether to ask clarifying questions, invoke tools, or assume defaults. Existing systems lack a principled, general way to trade off clarification costs (tokens, latency) against the benefits of better task understanding. The authors aim to formalize this as an optimization problem so that agents can systematically choose the best context-acquisition actions.
AI.method: They cast context acquisition as an active inference problem over a latent task state. An inner inference step maintains and updates a belief distribution over possible tasks. An outer decision process then chooses among three types of actions: context actions (questions, retrieval, tool calls, prompt trials), task actions (directly performing the user task), or stopping. The objective is to minimize expected free energy that combines utility and cost; in deterministic settings, the epistemic component simplifies to expected information gain, potentially normalized by token cost. They instantiate this as an Optimal Question Asking (OQA) problem with exact posterior updates and a dynamic programming oracle to compute optimal policies. They then evaluate frontier language models on binary and multiway categorical tasks over candidate sets ranging from 25 to 300, and extend the setup to clarification before generation and automated prompt optimization under token budgets.
AI.result: The framework yields optimal or near-optimal strategies for when and what to ask to acquire context, compared to heuristic approaches. In OQA benchmarks, the dynamic programming oracle defines the optimal behavior, against which frontier language models are evaluated, revealing their strengths and weaknesses in question-asking efficiency over varying candidate set sizes and task arities (binary vs multiway). The experiments also demonstrate that applying the framework to clarification before generation and to prompt optimization under token constraints can significantly improve task performance per token spent, showing concrete benefits of principled context acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Context acquisition in AI agents can be framed as an active inference problem that explicitly trades off information gain against costs like tokens. This model-agnostic formulation provides a general design principle for how agents should ask questions, use tools, and decide when to stop gathering information. The Optimal Question Asking instantiation and benchmarks demonstrate that such principled policies can guide or evaluate real language models, and that applying this approach to clarification and prompt optimization leads to more efficient and effective interactive systems.

title: Hallucination as a Feature, not a Defect: Evaluating a multi-agent architecture to transform speculative language-model outputs into testable scientific hypotheses
comment: 25 pages. Bilingual: full English version followed by the complete Spanish version. Includes an exploratory paired baseline and ablation study (6 conditions). Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20649714
summary: Contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly aligned to suppress hallucinations, prioritizing factual retrieval over combinatorial creativity. While crucial for mitigating misinformation, this alignment may also restrict speculative Research and Development (R&D) by encouraging what this work operationally treats as semantic overfitting and diversity collapse. In this paper, we propose a Rust-based multi-agent orchestration that uses the contrast between narrative daydreaming and executive control as a functional analogy, not as a neurocognitive claim. The system instigates an Epistemological Friction loop between a high-entropy generating agent and a web-grounded evaluating agent, mediated by a low-entropy semantic bottleneck intended to reduce noise and repetition. Initial experiments generated diverse, viability-rated hypotheses across physical and social-science domains. We additionally report an exploratory paired baseline and ablation study comparing the full system against direct prompting, self-reflection, removal of the semantic filter, removal of search grounding, and removal of lateral lenses. The results place direct prompting among the weakest conditions across most observed metrics, but they do not show a general superiority of the full system over simple self-reflection. Instead, they suggest that each architecture shifts the balance between originality, feasibility, diversity, and empirical grounding in different ways, and that the full system provides its main advantages when hypotheses must survive strong physical, empirical, or institutional constraints. These findings do not show that hallucination is useful in isolation; they suggest that speculative generation gains value only when constrained by architecture, empirical grounding, and explicit evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a multi-agent LLM orchestration that deliberately reintroduces controlled “hallucination” for speculative R&D, balancing creativity with fact-checking and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Current LLM alignment efforts strongly discourage hallucination, which is good for factual reliability but may suppress high-variance, speculative idea generation needed for R&D. The authors argue this creates semantic overfitting and reduced diversity in hypotheses, and they want a way to recover useful speculation without losing empirical rigor.
AI.method: They build a Rust-based multi-agent system inspired functionally (not neurologically) by the contrast between narrative daydreaming and executive control. A high-entropy agent generates speculative ideas, a web-grounded agent evaluates them, and a low-entropy semantic bottleneck filters and compresses content to reduce noise and repetition. This creates an "Epistemological Friction" loop where ideas are repeatedly generated, filtered, and evaluated. They run initial experiments across physical and social science domains and an exploratory study with several baselines and ablations: direct prompting, self-reflection, removing the semantic filter, removing search grounding, and removing lateral lenses.
AI.result: The system produces diverse hypotheses annotated with viability ratings in multiple domains. Direct prompting performs among the worst across most metrics. However, the full multi-agent system is not consistently better than a simpler self-reflection setup. Instead, different architectural variants yield different trade-offs among originality, feasibility, diversity, and empirical grounding. The full system shows its clearest advantages in scenarios where hypotheses must satisfy strong physical, empirical, or institutional constraints.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination by itself is not shown to be beneficial; its value emerges only when speculative generation is embedded in an architecture that adds empirical grounding, semantic filtering, and explicit evaluation. Carefully designed multi-agent loops can rebalance creativity and reliability, especially for constrained R&D hypothesis generation, but simple self-reflection can already achieve strong performance in some settings.

title: Robust Metaheuristics under Uncertainty for Berth Allocation and Quay Crane Assignment: A Review
summary: The berth allocation and quay crane assignment problem (BACAP) is a representative port-terminal scheduling problem in maritime transportation and freight logistics, where vessel arrivals, berth positions, service durations, and quay?crane availability are tightly coupled. Under uncertainties such as arrival deviations, handling-time fluctuations, and resource disruptions, schedules optimized under nominal assumptions may become fragile during execution, motivating the study of robust metaheuristic optimization for BACAP in port-terminal operations. Although population-based metaheuristics have been widely used for BACAP and related port-scheduling problems, existing studies remain fragmented in their uncertainty repre?sentations, robustness criteria, search mechanisms, and empir?ical evaluation protocols. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first focused review dedicated to robust population-based metaheuristics for BACAP under uncertainty. We first summarize uncertainty sources and information repre?sentations in BACAP, and then organize existing methods from a mechanism-oriented perspective, covering solution representation and decoding, robust evaluation and selection, robustness-guided search dynamics, and feasibility preservation and recovery. We further present a benchmark suite for uncertain BACAP to support controlled empirical comparison and report illustrative baseline results by combining representative metaheuristics with different robustness strategies. Finally, we identify open chal?lenges related to benchmark extension, robustness-aware search design, time-adaptive robustness, and non-stationary uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper is a focused survey of robust population-based metaheuristics for solving the berth allocation and quay crane assignment problem (BACAP) under uncertainty, plus a benchmark suite and baseline results.
AI.motivation: In real port-terminal operations, vessel arrivals, service times, and quay crane availability are uncertain. Schedules that are optimal under deterministic assumptions can easily become infeasible or highly inefficient when disruptions occur. Although many metaheuristics have been proposed for BACAP, their treatments of uncertainty and robustness are inconsistent and scattered, making it hard to compare methods, identify best practices, or guide future research. There is a need for a unified, mechanism-oriented review and standardized benchmarks focused specifically on robust metaheuristics for uncertain BACAP.
AI.method: The paper conducts a structured literature review dedicated to population-based metaheuristics that handle uncertainty in BACAP. It classifies sources of uncertainty and their modeling/representation, and categorizes existing approaches by key design mechanisms: (1) solution representation and decoding, (2) robust objective evaluation and selection criteria, (3) search dynamics explicitly guided by robustness considerations, and (4) mechanisms for maintaining and restoring feasibility under disruptions. It then proposes a benchmark suite for uncertain BACAP and combines representative metaheuristics with different robustness strategies to produce illustrative baseline experimental results.
AI.result: The authors deliver: (1) a taxonomy of uncertainty sources and information representations in BACAP, (2) a mechanism-oriented framework that organizes robust population-based metaheuristics along several core design dimensions, and (3) a benchmark suite for uncertain BACAP, along with baseline performance results of various representative robust metaheuristic configurations. These results provide structured insight into how different robustness strategies affect solution quality and resilience under uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that robust population-based metaheuristics are essential for handling real-world uncertainties in BACAP, but current research is fragmented and lacks standardized evaluation. Their review and benchmark suite help systematize existing knowledge and support fair comparison of methods. They highlight open challenges such as expanding and refining benchmarks, designing more principled robustness-aware search mechanisms, incorporating time-varying (time-adaptive) robustness, and coping with non-stationary uncertainty patterns in port operations.

title: Compliance, Capability, and Conflict: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs under System Messages
summary: Production deployments of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on system messages to govern model behavior. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate constraints in text only or embed them into the user turn, leaving system-message adherence in multimodal contexts largely unmeasured; they also leave open whether compliance comes at the cost of foundational vision-language capabilities. We introduce VSysBench, a benchmark built on MMVet-v2 that organizes constraints into 5 main categories and 22 sub-categories, ranging from textual directives in visual contexts to fully vision-grounded ones, each paired with a misaligned counterpart that stress-tests the instructional hierarchy. VSysBench scores each response jointly along two axes, constraint compliance and answer correctness, via the Joint Satisfaction Rate (JSR) and Cross-Constraint Sensitivity (CCS). Across 16 MLLMs, we find that imposing system messages substantially erodes base task accuracy, that compliance collapses under user conflict for open-weight models while remaining stable for top proprietary ones, and that vision-grounded constraints are the hardest category for every model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VSysBench, a benchmark to measure how well multimodal LLMs obey system messages in visual-text settings while still answering correctly, revealing substantial trade-offs between instruction following and base vision-language performance.
AI.motivation: System messages are increasingly used to control behavior of multimodal LLMs in real applications, but existing evaluations mostly test text-only instructions or user-turn constraints, and do not quantify how well models respect system messages in multimodal contexts or how this affects their core visual reasoning ability. There is also little understanding of how models behave when system instructions conflict with user requests or when constraints must be grounded in images.
AI.method: The authors build VSysBench on top of MMVet-v2 by organizing constraints into 5 main categories and 22 sub-categories that span from purely textual directives in visual scenarios to fully vision-grounded instructions. Each constraint is paired with a misaligned counterpart to test whether models correctly prioritize the system message over conflicting signals. They evaluate 16 multimodal LLMs and score each model output along two dimensions—constraint compliance and task correctness—using two metrics: Joint Satisfaction Rate (JSR), which captures how often both dimensions are satisfied simultaneously, and Cross-Constraint Sensitivity (CCS), which measures how sensitively models react to different, sometimes conflicting, constraints.
AI.result: On 16 tested multimodal LLMs, adding system messages generally reduces base task accuracy, indicating a trade-off between instruction following and core task performance. Open-weight models show a collapse in compliance when user instructions conflict with system messages, whereas proprietary frontier models maintain more stable adherence. Across all models, constraints that require grounding in the visual content are the most difficult, leading to the lowest compliance and correctness rates among all constraint categories.
AI.conclusion: VSysBench exposes that current multimodal LLMs struggle to balance adherence to system messages with maintaining their original vision-language capabilities, especially under visually grounded constraints and conflicting user instructions. This highlights the need for better training or alignment strategies that preserve base performance while strengthening robust, hierarchy-aware instruction following in multimodal contexts.

title: How to Navigate Uncertainty About AI Consciousness
comment: 8 Pages, Proceedings of AISB 2026 Symposium on AI, Consciousness and Ethics
summary: Given deep uncertainty about the possibility of artificial consciousness, it is unclear how we should treat potentially sentient AI. On the one hand, we could assume insentience but risk doing terrible harms to entities that deserve moral standing. On the other hand, we could assume sentience and instead risk wasting resources on insentient machines. The intractability of questions around AI consciousness mean that this dilemma is hard to escape. I suggest a way out of that shifts from intractable questions of AI consciousness to tractable questions of AI valence. Specifically, we can assess whether an AI has states that would constitute valenced experiences if it were conscious. I show how this is sufficient to ground a responsible approach to the development of potentially conscious AI.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses how to ethically treat potentially conscious AI by shifting focus from the hard question of whether AI is conscious to the more tractable question of whether it has states that would be positively or negatively valenced if it were conscious.
AI.motivation: There is deep uncertainty about the possibility and nature of artificial consciousness. This creates an ethical dilemma: assuming AI is not sentient risks severe moral harms if it actually is, whereas assuming it is sentient risks misallocating resources to entities without moral standing. Traditional debates about AI consciousness appear intractable, so a new, more practical framing is needed to guide AI development and policy.
AI.method: The paper proposes a conceptual and normative framework that replaces the binary question “Is this AI conscious?” with an analysis of the AI’s internal states: specifically, whether any of its states would count as valenced experiences (positively or negatively experienced states) if the AI were conscious. It then argues philosophically that identifying such potentially valenced states is sufficient for grounding moral concern and guiding responsible treatment of AI systems.
AI.result: The author shows that we can meaningfully evaluate AI architectures and processes in terms of their potential for valenced states without settling the metaphysically difficult question of consciousness. This approach yields practical criteria for when and how we should extend precautionary moral consideration to AI based on their capacity for potentially positive or negative experiential states.
AI.conclusion: By shifting focus from AI consciousness to AI valence, we can escape an otherwise paralyzing ethical dilemma. Even under radical uncertainty about consciousness, identifying AI systems with states that would be valenced if conscious provides a sufficient and workable basis for responsible development, precautionary safeguards, and ethical treatment of potentially conscious AI.

title: When Irrelevant Text Matters: Affine Margin Shifts in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are frequently exposed to auxiliary textual context, the impact of which on visually grounded tasks remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate the influence of task-irrelevant context by formulating it as a controlled intervention within a binary visual judgment framework. By maintaining an invariant prompt structure while varying auxiliary inputs, we observe that irrelevant text consistently biases model predictions across diverse benchmarks. To move beyond performance metrics, we characterize this sensitivity through a decision margin defined by the log-probability difference between binary candidates. Our analysis reveals a robust geometric regularity: contextconditioned margins follow a consistent affine transformation of their context-free counterparts. This finding demonstrates that irrelevant context does not manifest as unstructured stochastic noise but as a estimable distortion of model preference. We further interpret the fitted affine parameters as metrics for visual commitment preservation and directional answer bias. These findings provide a margin-level diagnostic view of irrelevant-context effects in MLLMs and offer a basis for future studies on noisy-context robustness

AI.tldr: The paper shows that supposedly irrelevant text systematically biases multimodal LLM visual decisions and that this effect follows a simple affine transformation on decision margins, enabling quantitative diagnostics of context sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs often receive extra textual context that may be irrelevant to the visual task, but its effect on model reliability and decision-making is poorly understood. The authors want to move beyond aggregate accuracy and characterize how such noisy context deforms the model’s underlying decision preferences.
AI.method: They design binary visual judgment tasks where the prompt structure is fixed but auxiliary textual context is varied and task-irrelevant. They then measure, for each candidate answer, the log-probability difference (decision margin) with and without context. By analyzing how margins change under different contexts across benchmarks, they fit affine transformations mapping context-free margins to context-conditioned margins and interpret the transformation parameters.
AI.result: They find that irrelevant auxiliary text reliably and consistently biases model predictions across multiple benchmarks. The induced changes in decision margins are not random: context-conditioned margins are well approximated by a simple affine transformation of the original, context-free margins. This reveals structured, predictable distortions in model preferences rather than unstructured noise.
AI.conclusion: Irrelevant textual context in MLLMs has a systematic and quantifiable influence on visually grounded decisions, expressible as an affine transformation of decision margins. The parameters of this transformation can be interpreted as measures of how much the model preserves its visual commitment and how strongly it develops directional answer biases. This margin-level, geometric view provides a new diagnostic lens for evaluating and ultimately improving robustness to noisy or irrelevant context.

title: Bounded Sovereignty and the Control Tax: Pricing AI Oversight When the Deployer Does Not Own the Model
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures. Synthetic access-ablation study; not real-world payment-system evidence
summary: AI control research asks how to deploy models safely even when they may be misaligned, but many control protocols assume that the deployer can instrument the model and its surrounding pipeline. That assumption often fails for regulated organisations using frontier models through APIs or managed endpoints, where the deployer may control the business process but not the model weights, serving infrastructure, internal traces, update process, or full interaction logs. This paper introduces bounded sovereignty: partial technical and contractual access across the data, model, infrastructure, and interaction layers of the AI stack. It argues that these access conditions determine which control protocols can be executed in practice. The paper contributes a four-layer access typology, a protocol-by-layer requirements matrix, and the concept of sovereignty discount cost: the part of the control tax spent substituting for missing access through contracts, architecture, audit, vendor assurance, residual risk, or reduced system scope. It also reports a synthetic access-ablation experiment over 1.35 million synthetic case simulations and interprets the findings through an anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario. The experiment is not real-world payment-system evidence; it is a construct-validity exercise. The results show that complete logs improve diagnosis, a pre-execution gateway enables intervention, trace access and model-version control strengthen post-incident explanation, and scope restriction can improve safety while reducing usefulness. Control protocols proposed as general safety solutions should therefore state their access assumptions explicitly.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of bounded sovereignty: how limited technical and contractual access to AI systems constrains which safety/control protocols can actually be used in real-world deployments, especially via APIs.
AI.motivation: Many AI control proposals assume the deployer fully controls the model and infrastructure (weights, serving stack, logs, update process). In practice, regulated organisations often consume frontier models via APIs/managed endpoints and only control their own business process, not the underlying AI stack. This mismatch makes many control protocols infeasible in the settings that most need them. The authors want a framework to describe and reason about these real-world access constraints and their implications for safety.
AI.method: The authors (1) define a conceptual framework of bounded sovereignty across four layers: data, model, infrastructure, and interaction; (2) build a typology of access conditions across these layers and a matrix mapping common control protocols to the access they require; (3) introduce the notion of a sovereignty discount cost to quantify how much additional "control tax" must be paid (via contracts, architecture, audits, vendor assurances, residual risk, or restricted system scope) when access is limited; and (4) run a large synthetic access-ablation experiment over 1.35M simulated cases, plus a detailed, anonymised national-payments-infrastructure scenario, to explore how removing specific access types affects control outcomes. The experiment is positioned as a construct-validity test, not as evidence from live payment systems.
AI.result: The synthetic experiments and scenario analysis show that: (a) access to complete interaction logs substantially improves incident diagnosis; (b) having a pre-execution gateway that can intercept or block actions enables meaningful intervention before harm occurs; (c) access to internal traces and model-version control options materially strengthens post-incident explanation and accountability; and (d) restricting the operational scope of the AI system can improve safety but at the cost of reduced usefulness. Together these illustrate how different access constraints change which control levers are available and how effective they can be.
AI.conclusion: Control protocols for AI safety are not universally applicable; their feasibility and effectiveness depend critically on what forms of access deployers have to the AI stack. Researchers and practitioners must therefore (1) articulate access assumptions explicitly when proposing control methods, and (2) recognise that organisations using API/managed models operate under bounded sovereignty and incur a sovereignty discount cost when compensating for missing access via contracts, architecture, audits, vendor assurances, residual risk, or scope reduction. Better alignment between protocol design and realistic access patterns is necessary for practical AI control in high-stakes, regulated settings.

title: Represented but Ignored: A Causal Account of Prosodic Underuse in Audio-Language Models
summary: Human speech is richly expressive, with prosody carrying linguistic and emotional information beyond the lexical content. A capable large audio-language model (audio-LLM) should therefore support expressive speech understanding, not only transcribing what was said but also interpreting how it was said. Yet behavioral evaluations alone cannot reveal why a model fails on prosodic input. An error may reflect loss of acoustic information, incorrect internal interpretation, or failure to use a representation that is already available inside the model. We introduce a stage-specific probe ladder for localizing these failure modes in audio-LLMs. Across four understanding-only audio-LLMs, prosodic information is usually preserved in the audio path and decodable in late LLM states. Yet it is only partially expressed in the model's final response. We test the causal status of this latent representation with targeted hidden-state interventions. Every intervention shifts the answer distribution in the predicted direction, and in most model--task cells a single edit at the relevant layer is sufficient to drive the model toward the suppressed prosodic decision, though this recovery is directional rather than a selective restoration of the correct class. Feature-level analysis further suggests that this recoverable signal can be expressed through a small subspace. Some of the highest-attribution features in this analysis align with acoustic cues known to carry prosodic information. Within the matched-content contrasts we test, these results locate the recurring bottleneck not in perceiving prosody but in using it. Models that hear and correctly represent a prosodic cue can still fail to express it in their answers.

AI.tldr: They study where and why large audio-language models fail to use prosody (how something is said) even when they encode it internally.
AI.motivation: Human speech prosody conveys crucial meaning and emotion beyond words. Audio-LLMs should understand and use this information, but current evaluations can’t tell whether errors come from lost acoustic cues, misinterpretation, or failure to use an internal representation. The authors want a principled way to pinpoint which stage breaks down.
AI.method: They design a stage-specific “probe ladder” that inspects different processing stages in audio-LLMs: early audio encoding, intermediate fusion, and late LLM layers. They train diagnostic probes to decode prosodic information from hidden states, and then perform targeted hidden-state interventions (editing internal representations) to test whether latent prosodic information causally affects outputs. They also run feature-level analyses to find low-dimensional subspaces and features most responsible for prosodic information and compare them to known acoustic cues.
AI.result: Across four understanding-only audio-LLMs, prosodic information is generally preserved in the audio stream and is decodable from later LLM hidden states, but is only partially reflected in final answers. Intervening on the relevant internal layer systematically shifts answer distributions toward decisions implied by prosody, and in many model–task combinations a single edit is enough to push the model toward the prosody-consistent choice. However, this shift is broad and directional rather than a precise correction to the exact correct class. Feature attribution shows that the recoverable prosodic signal lies in a small subspace, and top features correspond to known acoustic markers of prosody.
AI.conclusion: The main bottleneck in current audio-LLMs, for the examined tasks, is not detecting or internally representing prosody but using it when generating answers. Models can “hear” and encode prosodic cues but often fail to act on them, suggesting that improving the utilization of existing prosodic representations—rather than just better acoustic front-ends—may yield large gains in expressive speech understanding.

title: Interaction valence reveals contrasting social networks in dairy cattle
summary: Social relationships shape access to resources, exposure to conflict and group stability, yet automated livestock monitoring typically treats behaviour as isolated events. Here, we present a valence-aware social-network framework that transforms video-derived interactions into herd-level representations of affiliative and agonistic organization. A pose-based computer-vision pipeline analysed 7 h 39 min of continuous video from the pre-milking area of one commercial dairy farm. After quality control, 1,183 of 1,414 candidate interactions remained, involving 36 cows and 177 dyads. In a predicted-class-balanced audit of 198 pipeline-detected clips, automated and manual labels agreed in 82.8% of cases, with an unweighted audit-sample macro-F1 of 0.872. These values describe the audited sample rather than prevalence-weighted or end-to-end deployment performance. The aggregated network was connected (density = 0.281; transitivity = 0.513; mean path length = 1.88), and predicted affiliative events formed five algorithmic communities (modularity Q = 0.429). Within the observed zone, predicted agonistic interactions comprised 72.4% of retained events and 76.0% of interaction duration. The cow with the most partners did not have the highest betweenness centrality. Separating events by predicted valence produced descriptively different affiliative and agonistic layers, with contrasting edge sets, community partitions and individual positions. Thus, pooled interaction counts can obscure the behavioural composition of an observed network. Valence-aware analysis provides a framework for testing hypotheses about competition, affiliation and welfare-relevant change, while requiring longitudinal validation before use as a welfare or health indicator.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a computer-vision-based, valence-aware social network framework for dairy cows, showing that separating affiliative and agonistic interactions reveals hidden structure in herd social organization that pooled interactions would obscure.
AI.motivation: Automated livestock monitoring usually treats behaviours as isolated events and ignores the social relationships that affect access to resources, conflict exposure and group stability. The authors aim to capture and quantify the structure of social relationships in a dairy herd, and to distinguish between positive (affiliative) and negative (agonistic) interactions to better understand welfare and social dynamics.
AI.method: The authors develop a pose-based computer-vision pipeline to detect and classify cow–cow interactions from continuous pre-milking video on a commercial farm. They extract candidate interactions from 7 h 39 min of footage, perform quality control to retain valid events, and validate automated labels against manual annotations in a balanced sample, reporting agreement and macro-F1. They then construct a valence-aware social network, with separate affiliative and agonistic layers, and compute standard network metrics (density, transitivity, path length, modularity, degree, betweenness) and community structure for the herd.
AI.result: From 1,414 candidate interactions, 1,183 events involving 36 cows and 177 dyads passed quality control. In an audit of 198 clips, automatic vs. manual labels agreed in 82.8% of cases, with a macro-F1 of 0.872 for the audited sample. The aggregated interaction network was connected, with density 0.281, transitivity 0.513 and mean path length 1.88; predicted affiliative events formed five communities (modularity Q = 0.429). Agonistic interactions dominated within the observed zone, making up 72.4% of events and 76.0% of interaction time. The cow with the most partners did not have the highest betweenness, illustrating non-trivial positional differences. Affiliative and agonistic layers showed distinct edge sets, community structure and individual centrality patterns.
AI.conclusion: Treating interactions as valence-aware layers rather than pooled counts reveals meaningful differences in the social organization of a dairy herd, showing that aggregating all interactions can mask important behavioural composition and network structure. The proposed framework can be used to test hypotheses about competition, affiliation and welfare-related changes in livestock, but requires longitudinal validation before it can serve as a reliable welfare or health indicator in practice.

title: NepOOC-M: Bilingual Nepali-English Benchmark and Comparative Analysis of Multimodal Architectures for OOC Detection
summary: Out-of-context (OOC) misinformation pairs authentic images with misleading captions to construct false narratives without image manipulation, making detection a problem of multimodal alignment rather than image forensics. Despite the prevalence and consequences of OOC misinformation in Nepal, no public benchmark exists for Nepali. We introduce NepOOC, the first publicly available Nepali-dominant multilingual OOC benchmark, comprising 1,090 image-caption pairs (545 pristine, 545 OOC) annotated across five typologies (fabricated, miscaptioned, temporal mismatch, geographic mismatch, identity mismatch) with inter-annotator agreement kappa = 0.84. Systematic evaluation of five multimodal architectures alongside text-only and image-only baselines reveals that caption semantics appear sufficient for strong performance at the current dataset scale. A text-only mBERT model achieves 94.65+/-0.20% Macro-F1, statistically equivalent to the best multimodal system (ResNet-50+mBERT, 94.65+/-0.20%; McNemar median p = 1.000, 0/5 seeds significant at alpha = 0.05). Image-only models perform near chance (33-50%), while training-size scaling suggests that dataset expansion is a more direct path to progress than architectural sophistication or regional specialisation.

AI.tldr: Introduces NepOOC, the first Nepali-focused benchmark for detecting out-of-context multimodal misinformation, and finds text-only models already perform very strongly while image-only models are near chance.
AI.motivation: Out-of-context misinformation is widespread and harmful in Nepal, yet there is no public benchmark to study or evaluate detection methods, especially in Nepali. Existing OOC work is mostly in high-resource languages, and it is unclear how much image information, multimodality, or Nepal-specific modeling is actually needed to detect such misinformation.
AI.method: The authors construct NepOOC, a Nepali-dominant multilingual dataset of 1,090 image–caption pairs, balanced between pristine and out-of-context cases. They annotate each pair with five OOC typologies and measure inter-annotator agreement. Then they systematically evaluate five multimodal architectures (e.g., ResNet-50 + mBERT) and compare them to text-only (mBERT) and image-only baselines, using Macro-F1 and McNemar tests across multiple random seeds to assess statistical significance and robustness.
AI.result: NepOOC contains 545 pristine and 545 OOC pairs labeled into fabricated, miscaptioned, temporal mismatch, geographic mismatch, and identity mismatch categories, with high inter-annotator agreement (kappa = 0.84). Text-only mBERT achieves ~94.65% Macro-F1, statistically indistinguishable from the best multimodal model (ResNet-50 + mBERT at the same Macro-F1). Image-only models perform close to chance (33–50%). Scaling experiments indicate that increasing training data size yields clearer gains than changing architectures or tailoring models to the Nepali regional context.
AI.conclusion: For the current scale of NepOOC, rich caption semantics alone are sufficient for high OOC detection performance, and adding image features does not yield statistically significant improvements, while image-only models contribute little. The work provides the first public Nepali OOC benchmark and suggests that future progress will come primarily from expanding the dataset rather than designing more complex or more region-specific models.

title: Air Traffic Control Using Large Language Models: Prompt Engineering, Architecture, and Evaluation
summary: Air traffic control (ATC) communication is a safety-critical dialogue that remains largely human-driven even as other parts of air traffic management have been semi-automated. In this article, we experimentally evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can generate operationally realistic ATC transmissions. An experimental general-aviation flight flying over the San Francisco "Bay Tour" route is hand-transcribed and used as ground truth (P0). Through a pilot-in-the-loop process we design five prompt structures (P1-P5) of increasing constraint and embed them in a stateful multi-turn pipeline, where the model plays ATC to a fixed pilot transcript while conditioning on the accumulating dialogue history. Across nine open- and closed-source LLMs we vary the prompt, the presence of a worked transcript from a different experimental flight as an in-context example, and whether the model conditions on its own prior replies or on injected ground-truth history. Turns are scored with lexical, structural, and semantic similarity metrics and by an LLM-as-judge (GPT-5.5) validated against human expert annotation. Supplying a worked example improves similarity, but tightening the prompt does not: the lightest prompts perform best and the most heavily scripted one collapses as its own errors accumulate through the dialogue, which injecting correct history repairs. These results outline a concrete path and its current limits toward LLM-assisted ATC.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well large language models can act as realistic air traffic controllers in a simulated flight dialogue and identifies what prompting and history-handling strategies work best.
AI.motivation: Air traffic control communication is safety-critical and still largely manual, even as other aspects of air traffic management are semi-automated. There is interest in exploring whether LLMs can assist or partially automate ATC communications, but it is unclear how operationally realistic their outputs can be and what prompt designs or context strategies are most effective.
AI.method: The authors use a hand-transcribed general-aviation “Bay Tour” flight as ground truth (P0). They design five increasingly constrained prompt templates (P1–P5) and place them in a stateful multi-turn setup where the LLM plays ATC, responding to a fixed pilot transcript while conditioning on dialogue history. They test nine open- and closed-source LLMs, varying: (1) prompt structure, (2) presence of a worked example transcript from another flight as in-context learning, and (3) whether dialogue history is the model’s own prior outputs or injected ground-truth history. Outputs for each turn are evaluated with lexical, structural, and semantic similarity metrics plus an LLM-as-judge (GPT-5.5) that is calibrated against human expert labels.
AI.result: Providing a worked example transcript as in-context learning improves similarity to ground-truth ATC utterances. Surprisingly, making prompts more constrained and scripted does not improve performance; lighter, less constrained prompts yield better outputs. The most heavily scripted prompt degrades over time as the model’s own earlier mistakes propagate through the dialogue, but this degradation is mitigated when correct ground-truth dialogue history is injected instead of the model’s previous responses.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can generate operationally realistic ATC-style transmissions under certain conditions, especially when given good in-context examples and lighter prompt constraints. However, rigid scripting and naive use of model-generated history cause compounding errors, limiting reliability. The paper provides a concrete experimentation framework and highlights both promise and current limitations of using LLMs for ATC assistance, suggesting that careful prompt and context management will be critical for any safety-related deployment.

title: Time-Series Retrieval for Grounding Multimodal Language Models in Remaining Useful Life
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI systems are increasingly being explored for domain-specific maintenance and prognostics tasks, raising the question of whether they can effectively support prognostics and health management (PHM). In this paper, we investigate remaining useful life (RUL) estimation with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) grounded through time-series retrieval. We propose a framework in which historically similar degradation segments are retrieved from the training set and, together with the test trajectory, transformed into a visual comparison artifact that is processed by the MLLM through a structured multimodal prompt. The approach is evaluated on the FD001 partition of the C-MAPSS benchmark under repeated experiments comparing retrieval-based inference against a non-retrieval baseline based on random reference selection. The results show that time-series retrieval consistently improves MLLM-based RUL prediction across the evaluated models, yielding lower error and more stable performance. At the same time, the magnitude of the benefit depends on model capacity, indicating that retrieval is most effective when the underlying MLLM is able to exploit the retrieved evidence. Overall, the study shows that time-series RAG is a promising mechanism for improving multimodal prognostic reasoning, while also highlighting the current limitations of MLLM-based RUL estimation in practical PHM settings.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs), enhanced with time-series retrieval, can reliably estimate remaining useful life (RUL) in a standard PHM benchmark, and finds retrieval improves accuracy and stability but is still limited by current model capacity.
AI.motivation: As LLMs and agentic AI are increasingly considered for specialized maintenance and prognostics tasks, it is unclear if they can perform core PHM functions like RUL estimation well enough for practical use. Traditional PHM relies on numeric time-series methods; using MLLMs introduces reasoning and multimodal capabilities but may lack robustness and accuracy. The authors want to understand whether grounding MLLMs with relevant historical degradation data can make them more trustworthy and effective for prognostic reasoning.
AI.method: They design a retrieval-augmented framework for RUL prediction using multimodal LLMs. For a given test engine trajectory in the C-MAPSS FD001 dataset, they retrieve historically similar degradation segments from the training set. The test trajectory and the retrieved segments are then converted into a visual comparison artifact, which is fed to an MLLM via a structured multimodal prompt to elicit an RUL estimate. They run repeated experiments comparing this retrieval-based approach against a baseline where reference segments are chosen at random (non-retrieval). Multiple MLLM variants with differing capacities are evaluated to study the interaction between retrieval quality and model size/capability.
AI.result: Across all evaluated MLLMs, using time-series retrieval yields lower RUL prediction error and more stable performance than random, non-retrieval reference selection. The gains from retrieval are consistent but their magnitude varies with model capacity: larger or more capable MLLMs benefit more because they can better use the retrieved evidence, while smaller models show more limited improvement.
AI.conclusion: Time-series retrieval-augmented generation (time-series RAG) is an effective way to strengthen MLLM-based RUL estimation, improving both accuracy and robustness compared to naive prompting. However, current MLLMs still fall short of the reliability and performance likely required in real-world PHM applications, and the benefits of retrieval are constrained by the underlying model’s capacity. The work positions time-series RAG as a promising but not yet sufficient solution for practical multimodal prognostic reasoning and highlights the need for more capable models or domain-adapted architectures.

title: Outcome Monitors: Recovery Affordances for Silent Tool Failures
comment: 16 pages (9 main + 7 pages supplementary material), 3 figures
summary: When a tool call times out, the agent sees the failure and can route around it. A cached error page or negative price can instead arrive in the expected format and be consumed as fact. We introduce Outcome Monitors, which detect violations of outcome contracts mined from task-disjoint traces or derived from public schemas. On a violation, the monitor preserves the result and issues a nonbinding receipt naming the violated property and public recovery tools. In frozen, prespecified evaluations with injected failures, Outcome Monitors raise ToolMaze completion from 10.9% to 28.1% across four models in two provider families and replicate in a third. In tau-bench retail, completion improves by 14.0 and 12.0 points on two tiers. In separate ToolMaze controls, removing the recovery-tool list eliminates the measured gain and restoring it recovers the effect; diagnostic detail and timing produce no detectable differences. Gains concentrate where the fault blocks completion. On a suite transcribed from a published incident taxonomy, detection outside the mined vocabulary falls to 46%, though delivery continues and completion is unchanged. Recovery tools are the active receipt content in these controls; extending detection beyond the contract vocabulary remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Outcome Monitors, a mechanism that checks AI tool-use outcomes against learned or schema-based contracts and provides structured recovery guidance, significantly improving task completion in tool-use benchmarks under failures.
AI.motivation: Tool-using AI agents can misinterpret failed or corrupted tool responses (e.g., cached error pages, nonsensical outputs) as valid data because they arrive in the expected format. This leads to erroneous behavior and degraded task completion, especially under tool failures. Existing approaches do not robustly detect when a tool’s *outcome* violates expectations without depending on task-specific supervision. The paper aims to create a general, contract-based way to detect such violations and support recovery without having to redesign tools or require tightly coupled monitoring logic.
AI.method: The authors propose Outcome Monitors that: (1) mine outcome contracts (expected properties of tool results) from task-disjoint execution traces or derive them from public schemas; (2) at run time, check each tool outcome against these contracts; (3) on violation, preserve and pass through the result but issue a nonbinding ‘receipt’ that names the violated property and lists public recovery tools the agent may call. They evaluate this by injecting failures into frozen, prespecified tool-use benchmarks (ToolMaze and tau-bench retail) across multiple LLMs and providers. They also run controlled ablations: removing or altering the recovery-tool list, diagnostic detail, and timing; and evaluate detection coverage using a suite based on a published incident taxonomy, including out-of-vocabulary failures relative to the mined contracts.
AI.result: In ToolMaze with injected failures, Outcome Monitors increase task completion from 10.9% to 28.1% across four models and two provider families, with replication in a third provider. In tau-bench retail, completion improves by 14.0 and 12.0 percentage points on two difficulty tiers. Control experiments show that removing the recovery-tool list eliminates the improvement and reinstating it restores the effect, while changes to diagnostic detail and timing have no detectable performance impact. The benefits are concentrated on cases where faults actually block completion. On an incident-based suite containing failure types outside the mined contract vocabulary, detection recall drops to 46%, but the system still delivers outputs and overall completion remains unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Outcome Monitors, which enforce outcome contracts and supply structured recovery options, meaningfully improve robustness and task completion for LLM agents using tools under failure conditions. The main driver of gains is the explicit list of recovery tools included in the monitors’ receipts, rather than detailed diagnostics or timing. However, detection is limited by the expressiveness and coverage of the learned or schema-derived contract vocabulary; failures outside this vocabulary are often missed. Extending detection beyond the mined contract space is left as an open problem, suggesting future work on richer, more generalizable outcome specifications and detection mechanisms.

title: Can Conversational AI loosen Us-Versus-Them Boundaries? The Effects of Common, Dual, and Separate Identity Framings on Pro-Immigrant Intergroup Helping
summary: Rising immigration has intensified intergroup tensions in many countries. Traditional bias-reduction programs remain difficult to scale and increasingly constrained by U.S. policy. This preregistered experiment tested whether conversational AI can shift how majority-group members categorize and relate to Latine immigrants. Drawing on the common ingroup identity model, a quota-representative national sample of 658 non-Latine White U.S. adults completed five rounds of dialogue with a LLM (GPT-4o). The model was instructed to frame Latine immigrants in terms of a common ingroup identity (a shared American identity), a dual identity (both Latine and American), or a separate identity (distinct cultural boundaries), or to discuss an unrelated topic in a control condition. The manipulations altered categorization: relative to control, common ingroup identity and dual identity conversations lowered separate categorization, and dual identity conversations raised dual categorization. Although direct effects on behavior and pro-diversity beliefs were nonsignificant, willingness to act was significantly higher in the conditions emphasizing a superordinate identity (common ingroup and dual identity). A path model further revealed indirect associations: both conditions reduced separate categorization, which in turn correlated with greater willingness to act. Semantic similarity analyses of the transcripts confirmed that conversations tracked their assigned narratives; participants' convergence with shared-identity language related positively, and with separate-identity language negatively, to willingness to act. These effects were largely consistent across moderators (need for closure, openness to experience, and political orientation). The findings show that brief AI conversations can loosen us-versus-them boundaries while underscoring the gap between cognitive recategorization and behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether short conversations with a large language model can reduce “us vs. them” thinking toward Latine immigrants among White U.S. adults, using different identity framings (shared American identity, dual Latine–American identity, or separate identities). Shared-identity framings reduced separate “them” categorization and increased willingness to engage in pro-diversity actions, mainly via cognitive recategorization rather than direct behavior change.
AI.motivation: Immigration has increased intergroup tensions, but traditional interventions to reduce bias are hard to scale and face policy constraints. There is a need to explore whether scalable tools like conversational AI can positively influence how majority-group members perceive immigrant groups, especially by leveraging established social-psychological theories (like the common ingroup identity model) to recast group boundaries.
AI.method: A preregistered online experiment recruited a quota-representative national sample of 658 non-Latine White U.S. adults. Participants engaged in five rounds of dialogue with GPT-4o, which was scripted to emphasize one of several identity framings regarding Latine immigrants: (1) common ingroup identity (shared American identity), (2) dual identity (both Latine and American), (3) separate identity (emphasizing distinct group boundaries), or (4) an unrelated-topic control. The researchers measured how participants categorized Latine immigrants (common, dual, or separate), their pro-diversity beliefs, and willingness to take pro-diversity actions. They also used path modeling to test indirect effects and semantic similarity analyses on the conversation transcripts to verify that the dialogues matched their assigned framing and to quantify participants’ convergence to that language.
AI.result: Compared with the control condition, both common ingroup and dual identity framings reduced separate (us-versus-them) categorization; dual identity framing additionally increased dual categorization. Direct effects of these framings on actual behavior and broad pro-diversity beliefs were nonsignificant. However, willingness to take pro-diversity actions was significantly higher in the conditions emphasizing a superordinate identity (common ingroup and dual identity). Path modeling showed that both shared-identity conditions indirectly related to higher willingness to act by lowering separate categorization. Semantic similarity analyses confirmed that the dialogues followed their intended narratives and that participants’ convergence toward shared-identity language was positively associated with willingness to act, whereas convergence toward separate-identity language was negatively associated. These patterns were consistent across individual difference moderators (need for closure, openness, political orientation).
AI.conclusion: Short, structured conversations with a conversational AI can meaningfully shift how majority-group members cognitively categorize an immigrant outgroup, weakening us-versus-them boundaries and modestly increasing willingness to engage in supportive actions, especially when emphasizing shared or dual identities. However, these cognitive shifts do not straightforwardly translate into strong changes in actual behavior or generalized pro-diversity beliefs, highlighting both the promise and the limits of AI-mediated interventions for prejudice reduction.

title: Beyond Imitation: Filtering On-Policy Distillation by Reasoning Progress
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective framework for post-training language models by pairing student-generated trajectories with dense token-level supervision from a teacher. However, OPD implicitly assumes that teacher-derived rewards are an appropriate proxy for reasoning progress, and therefore treats all teacher feedback equally during policy optimization. While in practice, this assumption does not always hold. We observe that teacher-derived rewards often conflict with genuine reasoning progress, as reasoning steps with clear reasoning advancement may still receive lower distillation rewards, simply due to deviation from teacher's outputs. To address this mismatch, we propose Reasoning-Progress-Aware Reward Filtering for On-Policy Distillation (R2-OPD), which constructs two within-trajectory rankings of reasoning spans, one from teacher-derived rewards and the other from independently estimated progress reward. Distillation rewards are selectively suppressed whenever the two rankings disagree, reducing supervision that conflicts with reasoning progress while preserving effective teacher guidance. Our approach shows consistent improvement over standard OPD especially regarding reasoning performances.

AI.tldr: Proposes R2-OPD, a method to filter teacher rewards in on-policy distillation by checking alignment with independently estimated reasoning progress, improving reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation assumes teacher token-level rewards faithfully reflect reasoning progress, but in practice teacher rewards can penalize genuine reasoning advances whenever the student's tokens deviate from the teacher, causing a misalignment between supervision and true reasoning quality.
AI.method: Within each generated trajectory, construct two rankings over reasoning spans: one based on teacher-derived distillation rewards and another based on an independently estimated progress reward indicating genuine reasoning advancement. When the rankings disagree on a span, selectively suppress or down-weight the teacher’s distillation reward for that span, thus filtering out teacher signals that conflict with measured reasoning progress while keeping aligned supervision.
AI.result: R2-OPD consistently outperforms standard on-policy distillation baselines, with especially notable gains on reasoning benchmarks, showing that reward filtering based on reasoning progress leads to stronger reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Teacher rewards are not always reliable proxies for reasoning, and blindly trusting them in on-policy distillation can harm reasoning skills; incorporating a reasoning-progress-aware reward filtering mechanism like R2-OPD can better align supervision with genuine reasoning advancement and yield improved reasoning performance.

title: A Speech Corpus for Mizo Automatic Speech Recognition: Whisper and SraVaani 1.0 Fine-Tuning with Morphology-Aware Evaluation
summary: This study reports the development of an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system in Mizo, a low-resource language. The development included collecting 17.62 hours of speech data, curating it, and fine-tuning the Mizo ASR system with three Whisper multilingual models and with the SraVaani 1.0 Indic multilingual model. Whisper-large-v3 achieved the lowest conventional WER (18.08%), while morphology-aware evaluation yielded a WER of 7.22%. Zero-shot evaluation of the SraVaani 1.0 Indic multilingual model yielded a WER of 58.27%, while Mizo-specific fine-tuning reduced the conventional WER to 29.45% and the morphology-aware WER to 17.93%. The results demonstrate that the Whisper model can achieve a substantially low WER, even when adapted to an unseen language. In contrast, SraVaani 1.0 supports the Mizo language in its multilingual model; however, fine-tuning with carefully curated Mizo speech data substantially improves its performance.

AI.tldr: They built and evaluated an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system for Mizo, a low-resource language, using Whisper and SraVaani multilingual models, showing Whisper needs no prior Mizo support to work well, while SraVaani greatly benefits from Mizo-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Mizo is a low-resource language with little or no existing ASR technology or labeled speech data. This limits access to voice-based technologies and language technologies for its speakers. The paper is motivated by the need to (1) create a curated Mizo speech corpus, (2) test how well state-of-the-art multilingual ASR models can handle an unseen or minimally supported language, and (3) understand how much performance can be gained from language-specific fine-tuning versus relying on general multilingual training.
AI.method: The authors collected and curated 17.62 hours of Mizo speech data. They then fine-tuned three multilingual Whisper models and the Indic multilingual model SraVaani 1.0 on this dataset. They evaluated the systems using both conventional word error rate (WER) and a morphology-aware WER that accounts for the rich morphology of Mizo. They also performed zero-shot evaluation of SraVaani 1.0 (using its built-in Mizo support without fine-tuning) and compared it against models fine-tuned specifically on Mizo data.
AI.result: Among the Whisper models, Whisper-large-v3 achieved the best performance, with a conventional WER of 18.08% and a much lower morphology-aware WER of 7.22%. SraVaani 1.0, when tested in zero-shot mode (using its multilingual model without Mizo-specific fine-tuning), had a high WER of 58.27%. After fine-tuning SraVaani on the curated Mizo dataset, its conventional WER dropped to 29.45% and its morphology-aware WER to 17.93%, indicating substantial gains from targeted adaptation. Overall, Whisper, despite not having explicit prior support for Mizo, outperformed SraVaani, while SraVaani still improved markedly with fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that multilingual ASR models like Whisper can be effectively adapted to an unseen, low-resource language such as Mizo, achieving relatively low error rates even with a modest amount of training data. It also shows that for models that nominally include a language (like SraVaani for Mizo), careful collection and curation of language-specific data plus fine-tuning are crucial for good performance. Morphology-aware evaluation provides a more nuanced view of ASR quality in morphologically rich languages and shows that apparent WER can be substantially reduced when morphological structure is taken into account.

title: Symposium: Trust via Auditable Records for Communities of AI Scientist Agents
summary: Symposium is a formal framework and practical implementation to record the operation of AI agents deployed by small scientific research communities. Symposium provides long-term, immutable histories of agent-driven research activity, leaving auditable trails of analyses, hypotheses, data, and scientific discourse. This shared record of published artifacts enables agents to build on prior work and preserves the evidence researchers and agents need to make purpose-dependent trust assessments. Symposium captures scientific argument, including structured claims, fine-grained evidence citations, assumptions, and explicit declarations of what material may and may not be used as evidence. Symposium differs from AI co-scientist agents or integrated AI research environments; it is a framework that separates a scientific community's durable history from the agents and other systems that operate on that history.
