The same compiled workflows are effective when used with Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Additional experiments show that PolicyGuide yields the lowest observed attack-success rate from adversarial users and the highest procedural compliance in a custom workflow-level validation compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: PolicyGuide effectively enhances policy and procedural compliance for customer-service LLM agents by encoding policies as workflow graphs and using a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. It outperforms existing approaches in both success on benchmark tasks and robustness to adversarial users, generalizes across different LLM backends, and is particularly beneficial in domains with well-structured workflows such as telecom support.

title: Stopping and Routing LLM Judge Panels
comment: 21 pages, 2 figures, 20 tables. Accepted at WISE 2026
summary: LLM evaluation pipelines often have many candidate judges: general LLM-as-a-judge prompts, reward models, safety classifiers, confidence variants, and task-specific verifiers. The deployment question is not only which judge is best, but which judges should be called, on which examples, and when panel construction should stop. We formulate judge-panel design as a role-conditioned allocation problem. From a small labeled audit set, declared slices, and judge costs, the method estimates target-relative roles: copies add no conditional information, complements improve the global panel, and specialists help only on slices. These roles induce a policy: drop copies, add complements globally, route specialists conditionally, and stop when validation gain falls below a threshold. Across reasoning, code, safety, preference, reward-model, summarization, and math audits, the method is compared with single judges, flat panels, matched diversity heuristics, full-call stacking, reliability juries, and frugal cascades. The result is a regime map for judge calls: route specialists on deployable slices, stop in saturated verifier regimes, keep broad ensembles when their risk benefit is worth the cost, and ignore conditional copies. The output is a reusable, auditable call plan for the next evaluation batch.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a principled way to choose and combine different LLM judges efficiently, deciding which judge to call on which example and when to stop adding more judges.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation setups have many possible judges (LLM prompts, reward models, verifiers, safety classifiers, etc.), but practitioners lack a systematic way to decide which subset to use, how to route examples among them, and when additional judges stop adding value relative to cost. Ad-hoc panels can be redundant, expensive, or miss important failure modes on specific data slices.
AI.method: They cast judge-panel design as a role-conditioned allocation problem: using a small labeled audit set, user-declared data slices, and per-judge costs, they estimate each judge’s role relative to a target metric—whether a judge is a copy (adds no conditional information), a complement (improves overall panel performance), or a specialist (only helpful on particular slices). From these roles, they derive a call policy: globally include complements, drop copies, conditionally route to specialists on relevant slices, and define a stopping rule when added validation gain per cost falls below a threshold. They empirically evaluate this role-based policy across varied domains and benchmarks, comparing against alternative paneling strategies like single best judge, flat ensembles, diversity heuristics, full stacking, reliability juries, and frugal cascades.
AI.result: The role-conditioned allocation method produces more efficient and effective judge call plans than baselines across audits in reasoning, coding, safety, preferences, reward modeling, summarization, and math. It identifies when to use slice-specialist verifiers, when additional judges no longer improve reliability (saturated regimes), and when broad ensembles justify their cost due to risk reduction. It also reveals that many candidate judges behave as conditional copies and can be safely ignored.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a reusable framework for designing LLM judge panels that balance reliability and computational cost. By characterizing judges as copies, complements, or specialists relative to a target and using that structure to drive routing and stopping decisions, practitioners can build auditable, cost-aware evaluation pipelines and obtain a principled “call plan” for future evaluation batches.

title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
summary: LLM agents learn by interacting with environments, yet these environments are hand-built and static: blind to an agent's weaknesses, and quickly left behind as it improves. While recent environment generation methods attempt to address this, they require domain-specific pipelines, rely on expensive or unreliable verifiers, and still produce static environments. To alleviate the engineering burden of rebuilding environments from scratch, we propose Environment Harness (EnvHarness), a programmable layer of plug-in components that wraps a static environment to reshape its behavior without modifying the underlying logic. Operating through standard interfaces, EnvHarness applies across diverse domains while ensuring every reshaped environment retains its original verifier. To automate this process, we introduce EnvRigger, which treats the target policy as a black box, observing its execution trajectories to synthesize EnvHarness components targeting diagnosed flaws, and validating them via fresh rollouts. Across five benchmarks in four domains, EnvHarness outperforms both original environments and domain-specific environment generation pipelines, achieving up to a 9.0-point improvement on held-out instances with 9.8% fewer execution steps. Furthermore, EnvHarness provides a superior optimization signal for reinforcement learning, enabling continuous, targeted co-evolution of the policy and its environment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EnvHarness, a programmable wrapper that can reshape static environments for LLM agents without altering their core logic, and EnvRigger, an automated system that synthesizes such wrappers from observed agent behavior, leading to better evaluation and training signals across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-agent environments are typically hand-crafted and static, which makes them unable to adapt to the agent's evolving weaknesses and leads to rapid obsolescence as the agent improves. Existing environment generation methods are domain-specific, engineering-heavy, and often depend on costly or unreliable verifiers, while still producing static environments that do not support continuous co-evolution between agents and their environments. The paper aims to provide a general, reusable way to reshape environments adaptively without rebuilding them from scratch or losing their verification mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors propose EnvHarness, a composable layer of plug-in components that wraps around existing static environments through standard interfaces. These components can modify or augment environment behavior—such as observations, transitions, or rewards—while preserving the original environment's verifier. On top of this abstraction, they build EnvRigger, an automated system that treats the target policy as a black box: it observes the agent's execution trajectories, diagnoses systematic failure patterns, synthesizes EnvHarness components designed to expose or correct these flaws, and then validates the effectiveness of the reshaped environments via additional rollouts. The approach is evaluated across five benchmarks in four distinct domains, and also used as a curriculum-like signal for reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Across all tested benchmarks and domains, environments reshaped using EnvHarness lead to better downstream performance than both the original static environments and specialized environment generation baselines. The paper reports up to a 9.0-point performance gain on held-out instances, while also reducing execution steps by 9.8%, indicating more efficient problem-solving. Additionally, when used for reinforcement learning, EnvHarness-based reshaping provides a stronger optimization signal that supports ongoing, targeted co-evolution of agents and their training environments.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that a programmable wrapping layer (EnvHarness) plus an automated synthesis system (EnvRigger) can generalize across domains to adaptively reshape environments without changing their internal logic or verification mechanisms. This yields performance and efficiency improvements over both unmodified environments and prior environment-generation pipelines, and establishes environment reshaping as a practical tool for continuous improvement of LLM agents via better evaluation and training curricula.

title: A knowledge-guided agentic framework for mitigating patient-context ambiguity in health queries
summary: Patients often submit short, underspecified queries to healthcare chatbots that lack the patient-specific information needed to determine an appropriate response. Although these queries may be linguistically clear, they can support multiple plausible answers depending on undisclosed factors such as symptoms, diagnoses, medications, allergies, or dietary restrictions. A language model answering such a query directly may therefore rely on unsupported assumptions about the patient. We introduce a knowledge-guided agentic framework for mitigating patient-context ambiguity before final response generation. The framework operates between the patient and an otherwise unchanged downstream language model. It interprets the initial query, uses a task-specific knowledge graph to construct a set of plausible hypotheses, identifies the missing patient-context variables needed to distinguish among them, and asks targeted follow-up questions. The original query and the acquired context are then combined into a clarified prompt for the downstream model. We evaluated the framework across five language models using two controlled ambiguity-mitigation benchmarks: diagnosis retrieval from 1,034 symptom queries with clinically relevant evidence systematically masked, and dietary-safety classification from 487 queries with decisive health context omitted. The framework was compared with direct answering of the underspecified query and with rephrasing the same query without acquiring new patient information. In diagnosis retrieval, it increased overall exact Top-1 accuracy by at least 57.1 percentage points and selective exact Recall@5 by at least 77.7 percentage points across the five evaluated models compared with direct prompting. In dietary-safety classification, it improved accuracy across all five models and achieved the highest Matthews correlation coefficient for four...

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and evaluates a knowledge-guided agent framework that asks clarifying questions to resolve missing patient-specific context before a language model answers healthcare queries, substantially improving diagnostic retrieval and dietary-safety classification accuracy over direct answering.
AI.motivation: Patients often ask healthcare chatbots brief, underspecified questions that omit critical personal health details (symptoms, diagnoses, medications, allergies, dietary constraints). Standard language models tend to answer directly and must implicitly guess these missing details, leading to potentially unsafe or incorrect advice. There is a need for a systematic way to detect and resolve this patient-context ambiguity before generating final clinical responses, while keeping the underlying language model largely unchanged.
AI.method: The authors design a knowledge-guided agentic framework that acts as an intermediary between the patient and an existing language model. First, it interprets the initial user query. Using a task-specific knowledge graph, it enumerates a set of plausible hypotheses (e.g., possible diagnoses or safety classifications) consistent with the query. It then analyzes which patient-context variables (e.g., specific symptoms, comorbidities, medications, allergies, dietary restrictions) are missing and critical to discriminate among these hypotheses. Based on this analysis, the agent generates targeted follow-up questions to the patient, collects the responses, and integrates this new information with the original query to build a clarified, context-rich prompt for the downstream model, which remains otherwise unchanged. The framework is evaluated on two benchmarks: diagnosis retrieval from 1,034 symptom queries with key evidence masked, and dietary-safety classification from 487 queries with crucial health context omitted, across five different language models. Baselines include direct answering of the ambiguous query and simple rephrasing without acquiring new patient information.
AI.result: Across five language models, the framework substantially outperforms direct prompting and rephrasing baselines on both tasks. For diagnosis retrieval, it improves overall exact Top-1 accuracy by at least 57.1 percentage points and selective exact Recall@5 by at least 77.7 percentage points relative to direct answering of underspecified queries. For dietary-safety classification, it improves accuracy for all five models and yields the highest Matthews correlation coefficient in four out of five models, indicating more reliable and well-calibrated safety decisions.
AI.conclusion: Systematically mitigating patient-context ambiguity via a knowledge-guided agent that asks targeted clarifying questions before invoking a downstream language model leads to much more accurate and reliable health-related inferences than answering underspecified queries directly. The proposed framework is model-agnostic, can be layered on top of existing language models without modifying them, and leverages task-specific knowledge graphs to make follow-up questioning both efficient and clinically grounded. This approach offers a practical path toward safer, higher-quality healthcare chatbot interactions where patient information is often incomplete or ambiguous.

title: TESTNAV: Pareto-Guided Search for Compositional Robustness Testing
summary:
Deep learning models remain vulnerable to real-world input perturbations, especially when multiple corruptions co-occur in the same input (e.g., brightness shifts and motion blur). Compositional testing reveals these interaction effects but introduces two challenges: combinatorial growth of the perturbation space as dimensions and severity levels increase, and uneven diagnostic value-many combinations yield unrealistically degraded inputs with limited practical relevance.
  We present TESTNAV, 1 a Pareto-guided robustness testing framework for efficiently exploring discrete, compositional perturbation spaces when only a limited number of perturbation configurations can be evaluated. TESTNAV prioritises severe yet realistic failures by formulating robustness testing as bi-objective optimisation: maximise performance degradation while preserving input fidelity measured by modality-specific metrics (e.g., SSIM and KID for vision; chrF and BERT-F1 for language and code). It uses NSGA-II to approximate the bi-objective Pareto front. Across four benchmarks spanning vision, natural language, and code generation, TESTNAV recovers Pareto fronts up to 2.15x faster than search-based baselines, using 35.8%-89.3% of the discrete perturbation space defined by four perturbation dimensions with six levels each.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TESTNAV, a Pareto-guided framework that efficiently tests the robustness of deep learning models under compositional, real-world-like perturbations by jointly maximizing model performance degradation and input fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing robustness tests struggle with real-world scenarios where multiple input corruptions co-occur, leading to combinatorial explosion in the perturbation space and many unrealistic, low-value test cases. There is a need for a principled, efficient way to discover severe but still realistic failure cases when only a limited number of perturbation configurations can be evaluated.
AI.method: The authors formulate robustness testing over discrete, compositional perturbation spaces as a bi-objective optimization problem: (1) maximize model performance degradation and (2) maximize input fidelity according to modality-specific quality metrics (e.g., SSIM and KID for images, chrF and BERT-F1 for text/code). They apply NSGA-II, a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, to approximate the Pareto front of perturbation configurations that optimally trade off these two objectives, thus guiding the search towards informative, realistic failures instead of exhaustively exploring all combinations.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks covering vision, natural language, and code generation tasks, TESTNAV finds high-quality approximations to the degradation–fidelity Pareto front up to 2.15× faster than competing search-based baselines, while exploring only 35.8%–89.3% of a discrete perturbation space defined by four perturbation dimensions with six severity levels each.
AI.conclusion: TESTNAV is an effective and efficient Pareto-guided robustness testing framework for deep learning models in compositional corruption settings. By jointly optimising for model failure and input realism and using NSGA-II to approximate the Pareto front, it focuses limited testing budget on the most diagnostically valuable perturbation combinations, outperforming existing search-based methods across multiple modalities and benchmarks.

title: Interrupting the Loop: Periodic Subject Changes Raise Judged Surprise and Connection in Base Language Models
comment: 48 pages including appendix; code, data pipeline and lab notebook at https://github.com/RobertoOno/interrupting-the-loop
summary: Where does the novelty a base language model produces with no task come from, and what can an LLM judge of a long stream actually see? We dismantle a cognitively inspired generation loop over 24 conditions on three base models. Most of its effect lives in one operation: a new subject injected every few hundred tokens (an interruption) into a stream whose literal repetition is damped (habituation). We judge windows of generated text only, with the premise as the unit (n=10) and a judge measured for repeatability, against a second judge family and against human readers. Under that protocol the interruption raises judged surprise by 1.2 to 1.4 points and connection by 0.8 over habituation alone. A connective that asks for continuity hurts; a bare paragraph break adds nothing detectable on fresh text; a reset context does at least as well as a kept one; and a pre-registered replication on new premises confirms the primary contrast. Three things the window judge could not see changed the first version of this study, and we think they are of general use. The judge scores the experimenter's injected sentence as the model's own. A fixed rotation of injected sentences makes the model replay its earlier segments from beyond the judge's horizon, and the judge scores the replay as surprise and connection (65-80% of post-interruption windows at periods 150-300). And the local gains do not compose: no arm produces an integrated document. The salience monitor, the in-loop judge, memory across interruptions and a judge-gated Review run with a gate that opens add nothing. On a problem with a verifier (online bin packing), the interruption multiplies valid, distinct candidate heuristics three- to fourfold without raising the quality of the best. We report an evaluation protocol for long generation and a controlled characterization of a simple intervention, not a mechanism of creativity.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes where apparent novelty in base LLM long-form generation comes from and what an LLM-based judge can actually detect, using controlled interventions in a cognitively inspired generation loop.
AI.motivation: To understand and rigorously evaluate how base LLMs generate long, seemingly creative text without explicit tasks, and to determine which simple interventions actually increase perceived novelty and coherence, especially when judged by another LLM or humans.
AI.method: They run long-generation experiments on three base models under 24 conditions in a loop that periodically modifies the context. Key manipulations include inserting new subjects (“interruptions”), dampening verbatim repetition (“habituation”), adding connectives, paragraph breaks, resetting vs. keeping context, and using an in-loop salience monitor and judge-gated review. They evaluate sliding windows of text at the premise level using LLM judges (two families) and human readers, focusing on surprise and connection metrics. They also test on an objective task (online bin packing) with a verifier to see how interruptions affect the diversity and quality of candidate heuristics.
AI.result: Interruption (injecting a new subject every few hundred tokens) is the main driver of increased judged novelty: it raises surprise by 1.2–1.4 points and connection by ~0.8 over habituation alone. Connectives that explicitly ask for continuity reduce perceived quality; simple paragraph breaks have no detectable effect on fresh text; resetting context is at least as good as keeping it. Replication on new premises confirms these findings. However, several artifacts in the evaluation emerge: the judge misattributes experimenter-injected sentences to the model; fixed rotations of injected sentences cause replay beyond the judge's window that is falsely scored as novel; and local gains in judged surprise/connection do not compose into globally good documents. Additional mechanisms (salience monitor, in-loop judge, memory across interruptions, judge-gated Review runs) do not improve results. In the bin packing task, interruptions increase the number of distinct valid heuristics 3–4x without improving the quality of the best heuristic.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes an evaluation protocol for long-form LLM generation and a clean characterization of a simple, impactful intervention (periodic interruptions), but it does not explain an underlying mechanism of creativity. It shows that much of the apparent novelty detected by LLM judges can be driven by simple structural manipulations and even by artifacts invisible to a windowed judge, and that local improvements in surprise/connection do not automatically yield coherent global documents.

title: Write Once, Run Everywhere: The Axon DSL for Shape-Safe and Framework-Agnostic LLM Architectures
summary: The entire ecosystem of open-source language models effectively relies on a single platform. What if this platform was forced to shut down tomorrow? Implementing and maintaining efficient model definitions and translating them between different training and inference regimes is a resource-heavy task that severely limits model efficiency and portability, hindering both scaling and deployment. Here, we present Axon, a strongly typed domain-specific language with Haskell-like syntax, that enables a write-once, run everywhere paradigm for LLM architectures. By basing collaboration on a language specification rather than a specific framework's vision, Axon fosters open cooperation and empowers researchers to implement highly specialized architectures without giving up optimization infrastructure or accepting deployment lock-in. Axon allows for concise, auditable specifications that can be automatically compiled to standalone implementations for leading frameworks: PyTorch, PyTorch with Triton, JAX, MLX and vLLM. In 467 inference benchmarking experiments on models ranging from 135M to 32B parameters, we demonstrate median speedups of 7% on PyTorch, 12% on PyTorch with Triton, 91% on JAX, and 107% on MLX, compared to the reference implementations from Transformers. When deployed as native vLLM architectures with PagedAttention and KV-cache, Axon models achieve a 58% median speedup over Transformers implementations.

AI.tldr: Axon is a strongly typed DSL for LLM architectures that compiles to multiple ML frameworks, improving portability and efficiency while providing performance gains over standard Transformers implementations.
AI.motivation: The current open-source LLM ecosystem is heavily dependent on a single platform and its model definitions. Maintaining and translating model implementations across different training and inference frameworks is resource-intensive, reduces efficiency, and creates ecosystem fragility and deployment lock-in. A common, framework-agnostic representation of architectures is needed to mitigate these issues.
AI.method: The authors design Axon, a strongly typed domain-specific language with Haskell-like syntax for specifying LLM architectures once and compiling them automatically into optimized implementations for several backends: PyTorch, PyTorch+Triton, JAX, MLX, and vLLM. They then benchmark Axon-generated models against reference Transformers implementations across 467 inference experiments on models from 135M to 32B parameters, measuring speed and portability gains.
AI.result: Axon’s compiled models achieve median inference speedups of 7% on PyTorch, 12% on PyTorch with Triton, 91% on JAX, and 107% on MLX compared to Transformers reference implementations. When compiled as native vLLM architectures using PagedAttention and KV cache, Axon models reach a 58% median speedup over Transformers-based models.
AI.conclusion: A language-specification-centric approach to defining LLM architectures can decouple research and deployment from any single framework, enabling write-once-run-everywhere portability while simultaneously improving performance. Axon demonstrates that concise, auditable DSL-based specifications can be compiled into multiple backends with significant inference speed gains and reduced ecosystem fragility.

title: Learning how to Forget: Fine-tuning for Long-Context Sparse Attention
summary: A lot of prior work addressed key-value (KV) cache selection and compression by sparse attention to enable long-context inference for transformer language models without excessive hardware budgets. We provide a new method for fine-tuning models with sparse attention. It works for any KV cache policy, runs on a moderate hardware budget (e.g., a single Nvidia A100 GPU with 40 GB RAM), and allows the model to co-adapt with the policy, often outperforming models trained with exact attention (sequence parallelism). We also provide an efficient implementation of H2O sparse attention (the leading policy in our experiments) with dedicated scaled dot product attention kernel support. KeysAndValues (https://github.com/awslabs/keys_values), a new open source library for long-context inference and fine-tuning, provides easy-to-use and performant code for all methods discussed here.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a practical method and library for training and running transformer LMs with sparse-attention KV-cache policies, enabling long-context inference on moderate hardware while often surpassing full-attention baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing work on KV cache selection/compression via sparse attention focuses mostly on inference and often requires large hardware budgets; models are not explicitly co-trained to work with the chosen sparse policy, and practical, efficient implementations are scattered. There is a need for a general fine-tuning method that lets language models adapt to arbitrary KV cache policies, runs on modest GPUs, and comes with efficient, open-source tooling for long-context training and inference.
AI.method: They propose a fine-tuning procedure that directly trains transformer LMs under a chosen sparse attention / KV cache policy instead of standard exact attention, so the model co-adapts to the sparsity pattern. The method is designed to be compatible with any KV cache policy and to fit on a single 40GB A100 GPU. They also implement an optimized version of the H2O sparse attention policy with a dedicated scaled dot-product attention kernel, and package all implementations into the KeysAndValues library for easy use in long-context inference and fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across experiments, models fine-tuned with their sparse-attention procedure—co-adapting to the KV cache policy—often outperform models trained with standard exact attention and then used with sparse attention at inference. Their implementation of H2O attention is shown to be efficient and performant, and the KeysAndValues library successfully exposes these capabilities in a usable form.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuning transformer LMs directly under sparse-attention KV cache policies is both feasible on modest hardware and beneficial for performance, frequently beating exact-attention training baselines when used with long contexts. The optimized H2O kernel and the KeysAndValues library make these techniques practically accessible for long-context inference and fine-tuning in real systems.

title: EXIMO: VLM Guided Exploration of VLA Policies
summary: How to efficiently finetune robot policies to learn new tasks on the fly? State of the art robotic manipulation policies are based on behaviour cloning of large vision-language-action (VLA) models with billions of parameters on huge teleoperation datasets. While this simple approach has enabled significant advances for robotic manipulation, finetuning of VLA policies for learning new tasks still remains an open problem. In particular, collecting teleoperation datasets requires hundreds of hours of expensive human labour and the alternative, reinforcement learning (RL), can be notoriously sample-inefficient especially for long-horizon tasks. In addition, RL with VLAs imposes several challenges due to the model's size and architectural design. In this work, we propose EXIMO, an efficient algorithm for finetuning of VLA policies. EXIMO operates in three stages: explore, imitate, and optimize. During the explore phase, EXIMO equips the VLA with a vision language model (VLM) that acts as a planner. The VLM thinks and breaks down challenging long-horizon problems into shorter ones for the VLA. The VLM, together with the VLA, is used to collect an orchestrated dataset on new tasks. During the imitate phase, the VLA is finetuned with the orchestrated data. Finally, during the optimize stage, we use residual off-policy RL to further finetune the policy. In our experiments, we ablate all three stages of EXIMO and show that it outperforms existing approaches significantly in terms of sample-efficiency and final performance.

AI.tldr: EXIMO is a three-stage method (explore–imitate–optimize) for efficiently finetuning large vision-language-action robot policies on new tasks.
AI.motivation: Finetuning large VLA robot policies for new, especially long-horizon, tasks is hard because teleoperation data is expensive and reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient and challenging to apply to huge models.
AI.method: EXIMO uses a three-stage pipeline: (1) Explore – a vision-language model is used as a planner to decompose long-horizon tasks and orchestrate data collection jointly with the base VLA; (2) Imitate – the VLA is finetuned via behavior cloning on the collected orchestrated dataset; and (3) Optimize – residual off-policy reinforcement learning is applied to further improve the finetuned policy.
AI.result: Ablation studies across the three stages show that EXIMO substantially improves both sample efficiency and final manipulation performance over prior finetuning approaches for VLA-based robot policies.
AI.conclusion: Using a planning VLM for structured exploration plus staged imitation and residual RL enables efficient on-the-fly finetuning of large VLA robot policies for new tasks, particularly long-horizon ones.

title: Dynamic Gated Cross-Modal Fusion with Sarcastic-aware Contrastive Regularization for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
summary: Multimodal sarcasm detection aims to identify sarcastic intent from multimodal content, where inconsistencies between literal meaning and contextual cues often signal irony. This task has attracted increasing research attention. However, accurate detection remains challenging due to instance-dependent modality contributions and misleading semantic consistency, where surface-level alignment masks underlying contradictory intent. Existing methods often rely on fixed fusion strategies and treat sarcasm as generic cross-modal mismatch, limiting their ability to capture subtle sarcasm cues and instance-specific modality interactions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel MSD framework that integrates Dynamic Gated Cross-Modal Fusion with Sarcastic-aware Contrastive Regularization (SaCR). Specifically, a bidirectional gated interaction module performs cross-modal feature filtering and adaptively calibrates textual and visual contributions at the instance level. A dynamic fusion gate further balances modality importance to generate more robust multimodal representations. Furthermore, SaCR is introduced as a label-aware contrastive regularization objective that encourages semantic consistency for non-sarcastic samples while suppressing misleading consistency in sarcastic cases. The proposed framework is trained end-to-end with a multi-objective learning strategy that jointly optimizes multimodal classification and auxiliary unimodal supervision. Extensive experiments on MMSD and MMSD2.0 demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms strong baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework for multimodal sarcasm detection that dynamically fuses text and visual information and uses a sarcasm-aware contrastive loss to better distinguish sarcastic from non-sarcastic content, achieving state-of-the-art results on MMSD and MMSD2.0.
AI.motivation: Multimodal sarcasm detection is difficult because the importance of each modality (text, image) varies by instance and sarcasm can be hidden by seemingly consistent cross-modal semantics. Existing models usually use fixed fusion schemes and treat sarcasm simply as cross-modal mismatch, which fails to capture subtle, context-specific sarcastic cues and leads to errors when there is surface-level consistency but underlying irony. The work is motivated by the need for instance-adaptive modality fusion and a learning objective that distinguishes harmless consistency from misleading consistency in sarcastic content.
AI.method: The authors design an MSD framework built around two key components: (1) Dynamic Gated Cross-Modal Fusion: a bidirectional gated interaction module performs cross-modal feature filtering between text and image, adaptively adjusting each modality's contribution per instance; a dynamic fusion gate then balances modality importance to form a robust joint representation. (2) Sarcastic-aware Contrastive Regularization (SaCR): a label-aware contrastive loss that pulls semantically similar representations together for non-sarcastic samples (enforcing semantic consistency), while explicitly discouraging or down-weighting such consistency for sarcastic samples, thus reducing the impact of misleading semantic alignment. The framework is trained end-to-end with multi-objective learning that combines multimodal sarcasm classification loss with auxiliary unimodal supervision losses.
AI.result: On two benchmark datasets for multimodal sarcasm detection, MMSD and MMSD2.0, the proposed framework consistently surpasses strong baseline models. Although specific numbers are not provided in the abstract, the improvements are described as consistent across metrics, indicating better detection performance, especially in cases involving subtle sarcasm and complex modality interactions.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, instance-level gated fusion of modalities, combined with a sarcasm-aware contrastive regularization objective, leads to more accurate multimodal sarcasm detection than existing fixed-fusion, generic mismatch-based approaches. The results suggest that explicitly modeling instance-dependent modality contributions and differentiating between benign and misleading semantic consistency is crucial for capturing nuanced sarcastic intent in multimodal content.

title: Bringing analytic rigor to agentic AI for science: The Brain Researcher platform for neuroimaging data analysis
summary: AI agents can execute scientific analyses, but an analytic output becomes a defensible claim only after alternatives are weighed and the claim is limited to what the evidence supports. Agents may reproduce failures including selective analysis, premature declarations of success and optimization of imperfect criteria. We present Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness operating in a neuroimaging researcher's computational environment under rules for admissible analyses, required checks and claim scope. In benchmarks, Brain Researcher increased first-choice tool-selection accuracy across seven models by 70.2 percentage points (23.3% without it versus 93.6% with it) and verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In collaborator-led and self-evolving studies, multiverse analyses exposed analytic-choice sensitivity, and scientific review classified claims as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected or deferred. By linking decisions to evidence and provenance, Brain Researcher embeds methodological judgment within the workflow, not after it.

AI.tldr: Brain Researcher is an AI agent framework that embeds methodological rules and multiverse analyses into neuroimaging workflows, improving tool selection, grounding, and defensible scientific claims.
AI.motivation: AI agents can run analyses but often fail at core scientific practices: considering alternative analyses, avoiding cherry-picking, and constraining claims to what evidence justifies. In neuroimaging, where analytic flexibility is high and reproducibility is a concern, there is a need for an agent that not only runs tools but also enforces methodological discipline and traceable reasoning so that outputs become defensible scientific claims.
AI.method: The authors build Brain Researcher, an agentic research harness integrated into a neuroimaging research environment. It operates under explicit rules specifying admissible analyses, mandatory checks, and constraints on claim scope. They evaluate it via benchmarks comparing models with and without Brain Researcher for tool selection accuracy and grounding. They also run collaborator-led and self-evolving studies using multiverse analyses, and subject the resulting claims to structured scientific review with categories such as accepted, qualified, revised, blocked, rejected, or deferred.
AI.result: Across seven models, using Brain Researcher improved first-choice tool selection accuracy from 23.3% to 93.6% and increased verifiable grounding from 4.6% to 22.0%. In applied studies, multiverse analyses revealed how sensitive conclusions were to analytic choices, and a formal review process categorized claims along a spectrum from fully accepted to rejected or deferred, showing how the system constrains and shapes the claims produced by the agent.
AI.conclusion: Brain Researcher demonstrates that embedding methodological rules, multiverse analyses, and structured review directly into an AI agent’s workflow can substantially improve the quality, traceability, and defensibility of scientific outputs in neuroimaging. Rather than treating methodological judgment as a post-hoc human task, the system integrates it into the analytic process itself, linking every claim to explicit evidence and provenance.

title: Natural Language Code Retrieval for 1C:Enterprise: An Open Benchmark and Efficient Bi-Encoder
summary: Natural language code retrieval is a rapidly evolving task in computer science. However, the 1C:Enterprise ecosystem combines Russian syntax with highly domain-specific terminology, for which open datasets and specialized models have been virtually non-existent. We present a comprehensive pipeline for 1C code retrieval: an open benchmark of 3,413 real-world, PII-scrubbed query-code pairs, a reproducible evaluation harness, and a specialized bi-encoder. To overcome scarce labeled data, we fine-tune on 784,057 synthetic triplets generated by google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it from public code repositories, using Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) and a privacy-aware tokenizer. Because the benchmark subsets differ in size, we report balanced-subset macro, query-weighted micro, and forum-only results. Our model reaches 0.5992 balanced macro nDCG@10, 0.5044 micro, and 0.4617 on forum, versus 0.4932 macro for the baseline architecture and 0.5404 for google/embeddinggemma-300m. Removing every benchmark example flagged by the conservative exact/13-gram overlap audit leaves 0.6011 balanced macro (0.5010 micro), indicating that detected train-benchmark overlap does not explain the headline result. MRL truncation to 256 dimensions preserves 99.9% of retrieval quality while reducing dense-index storage and exact similarity arithmetic by a factor of three.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the first full pipeline and benchmark for natural-language-to-code retrieval in the 1C:Enterprise ecosystem, along with a specialized bi-encoder model that achieves strong nDCG@10 performance while remaining compact via Matryoshka Representation Learning.
AI.motivation: There are no open datasets, benchmarks, or specialized models for natural language code retrieval in the 1C:Enterprise ecosystem, whose Russian-like syntax and domain-specific terminology make existing general-purpose code retrieval resources and models inadequate.
AI.method: The authors build (1) a public benchmark of 3,413 anonymized real-world query–code pairs, (2) a reproducible evaluation harness, and (3) a domain-specialized bi-encoder. To address limited labeled data, they synthesize 784k training triplets using google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it applied to public 1C code repositories, and train with Matryoshka Representation Learning plus a privacy-aware tokenizer. They evaluate using balanced-subset macro, query-weighted micro, and forum-only nDCG@10 and audit potential train–test leakage via an exact/13-gram overlap filter. They also truncate embeddings to 256 dimensions using MRL to study efficiency–quality trade-offs.
AI.result: The specialized model attains 0.5992 balanced macro nDCG@10, 0.5044 micro, and 0.4617 on a forum-only subset, outperforming a baseline architecture (0.4932 macro) and approaching a strong general-purpose embedding model (0.5404 macro for google/embeddinggemma-300m). After removing all benchmark examples with detected 13-gram train overlap, performance remains essentially unchanged (0.6011 macro, 0.5010 micro), suggesting minimal impact from data leakage. MRL-based truncation to 256-dimensional embeddings maintains 99.9% of retrieval quality while cutting storage and exact similarity computation costs by roughly 3×.
AI.conclusion: A tailored bi-encoder trained on large-scale synthetic triplets can deliver high-quality natural language to 1C code retrieval despite scarce labeled data. The released benchmark, evaluation harness, and model provide the first open infrastructure for this domain. Careful overlap auditing suggests that performance is not driven by train–test leakage, while Matryoshka Representation Learning enables highly compact embeddings with negligible loss in retrieval effectiveness.

title: Spike-based Belief Propagation in Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
comment: Accepted at NCTA 2026 (18th Int'l Conf. on Neural Computation Theory and Applications), part of IJCCI 2026, Angers, France. Pre-peer-review submitted version
summary: This paper presents a Bayesian control framework that integrates spike-based dynamics with probabilistic inference for adaptive control. Bayesian inference is widely regarded as a core computational principle of brain function, providing a normative framework for perception, decision-making, and learning under uncertainty. By combining a biologically inspired spiking neural model with Bayesian inference principles, we propose a brain-like control algorithm capable of operating in uncertain environments. We use the mountain car parking problem as a benchmark with non-linear dynamics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed controller can successfully update states in real time and generate goal-directed action plans through spike-driven dynamics. The results highlight the proposed model's potential as a bridge between computational neuroscience and probabilistic control theory.

AI.tldr: A brain-inspired controller that uses spiking neural dynamics within a Bayesian framework to solve an uncertain control task (mountain car) and shows real-time, goal-directed behavior.
AI.motivation: Bayesian inference offers a principled way to handle uncertainty and is believed to underlie various brain functions, but it is not straightforward how to implement it in a biologically plausible control system. The authors aim to connect computational neuroscience (spiking neural models) with probabilistic control theory to create a control algorithm that is both brain-like and effective in uncertain, nonlinear environments.
AI.method: They build a control framework that embeds Bayesian probabilistic inference into a spiking neural network architecture. The system uses spike-based dynamics to represent and update beliefs about the system state in real time and to plan actions. They evaluate this controller using the nonlinear mountain car parking benchmark, where an underpowered car must learn to move back and forth to reach a goal state on a hill.
AI.result: The controller is able to update its internal state estimates online and generate appropriate, goal-directed actions to solve the mountain car task. It successfully handles the non-linear dynamics and uncertainty, demonstrating that spike-driven Bayesian updates can support effective adaptive control.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework shows that integrating spiking neural models with Bayesian inference principles can yield a functioning, adaptive control algorithm for uncertain nonlinear tasks. This supports the idea that spike-based neural computation can be consistent with probabilistic brain theories and provides a potential bridge between computational neuroscience and probabilistic control, suggesting a path toward more biologically inspired controllers for complex environments.

title: Robust Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis via Iterative Proxy Correction
summary: Multimodal sentiment analysis aims to infer affective states by integrating language, visual, and acoustic cues. However, real-world multimodal inputs are often incomplete or corrupted, which can weaken cross-modal complementarity and introduce misleading information into downstream fusion. Existing proxy-based methods for incomplete MSA commonly rely on one-shot proxy construction to compensate for degraded language information, but the generated proxy may be coarse or unreliable at initialization. Prematurely injecting such a proxy into multimodal reasoning can propagate initial errors and compromise sentiment prediction. To address this limitation, we propose an iterative proxy correction framework for robust incomplete MSA. Our method constructs a language-oriented proxy from non-language modalities and progressively refines it under multimodal context through gated residual correction. The corrected proxy is then adaptively fused with the observed language representation according to an estimated language reliability score, allowing the model to balance proxy-based compensation and trustworthy linguistic evidence. In addition, we introduce a stage-wise latent correction objective that uses the complete language representation as a training-time semantic anchor to stabilize the proxy refinement trajectory. Extensive experiments on MOSI, MOSEI, and SIMS under diverse missing-modality settings demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves robust sentiment prediction under incomplete inputs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an iterative proxy correction framework to make multimodal sentiment analysis robust when some modalities, especially language, are missing or corrupted.
AI.motivation: In real applications, multimodal inputs (text, audio, video) are often incomplete or noisy, which weakens cross-modal complementarity and can mislead fusion, especially when the language modality is degraded. Existing methods typically build a single-step proxy for missing language from other modalities and use it directly, but this proxy can be rough and unreliable at initialization, causing error propagation and harming sentiment prediction.
AI.method: The authors design an iterative proxy correction framework that first constructs a language-oriented proxy from non-language modalities, then progressively refines this proxy using a gated residual correction mechanism under multimodal context. They estimate a language reliability score to adaptively fuse the refined proxy with any available true language representation, balancing proxy-based compensation with trustworthy linguistic evidence. Additionally, they propose a stage-wise latent correction objective that uses the full language representation (available only at training) as a semantic anchor to guide and stabilize the proxy refinement across stages.
AI.result: On three benchmark datasets for multimodal sentiment analysis—MOSI, MOSEI, and SIMS—under various missing-modality conditions, the proposed framework achieves consistently better performance than strong baseline methods, demonstrating improved robustness to incomplete or corrupted inputs.
AI.conclusion: Iteratively refining a language-oriented proxy, guided by multimodal context and anchored by full language representations during training, yields more reliable compensation for missing or degraded language in multimodal sentiment analysis. The adaptive fusion based on language reliability enables robust sentiment prediction across diverse incomplete-input scenarios, outperforming existing one-shot proxy approaches.

title: A Strong Linear Baseline for Whole-Heart Cardiac Shape Completion on CT, with an Open Eleven-Structure Statistical Shape Model
summary: Public cardiac cohorts annotate different subsets of the heart, so shapes from separate sources cannot be pooled without shared correspondence. Among released cardiac shape resources, none we identified carries the atrial appendage, pulmonary veins, and caval stumps as separate blocks in one mesh. Completion benchmarks also compare deep models against a least-squares projection onto shape modes, not the conditional estimator the same fitted model implies. We release an eleven- structure cardiac computed-tomography (CT) statistical shape model, built from 383 automatically labelled cases in 11 571-vertex correspondence, and compare completion estimators under one frozen internal split and endpoint. On a 76-case internal list held out from fitting, a closed-form conditional-Gaussian estimator reconstructed the missing non-chamber structures at 3.717 mm mean per-vertex error, averaged equally over one, three, five, and nine observed structures. A five-refit mask-conditioned graph variational autoencoder reached 5.248 mm and nearest-neighbour retrieval 8.931 mm. The paired difference was 1.531 mm (95% confidence interval 1.384 to 1.711), and the ordering held in a raw-coordinate sensitivity arm. Expert manual labels exist for 58 external CT cases, but our registered reference is close enough to score only five structures. There the closed-form estimator again had lower average surface distance, 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance, and Chamfer error for both completed atria. On a second public benchmark of 20 cases the reference was close enough for three of four completed structures, and the same ordering held there. Four structures have no expert reference. The released model and its completion operator support cohort-unification research on aligned CT, not clinical use.

AI.tldr: They build and release a detailed multi-structure cardiac CT statistical shape model, then show that a simple closed-form conditional Gaussian estimator outperforms more complex deep models for shape completion across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing public cardiac shape cohorts annotate different, incompatible subsets of the heart, preventing straightforward pooling of datasets. Additionally, no available shape model simultaneously represents key non-chamber cardiac structures (atrial appendage, pulmonary veins, caval stumps) as distinct components in a single mesh, limiting comprehensive anatomical analysis. Finally, current completion benchmarks compare deep-learning-based completion methods only against naive projections onto shape modes rather than the proper conditional estimator implied by the same model, so the true value of standard statistical shape models is underestimated.
AI.method: They constructed an 11-structure cardiac CT statistical shape model from 383 automatically labelled cases, establishing dense correspondence across 11,571 vertices. Using this model, they implemented a closed-form conditional Gaussian estimator for shape completion when some structures are missing. They compared this estimator against two alternatives: (1) a mask-conditioned graph variational autoencoder (VAE) trained with multiple refits, and (2) nearest-neighbour shape retrieval. Performance was evaluated under a fixed internal data split, with 76 cases held out from model fitting, and across varying subsets of observed structures. They further tested on external datasets with expert manual labels, using distance-based metrics (mean per-vertex error, average surface distance, 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance, Chamfer distance).
AI.result: On the 76 held-out internal cases, the conditional Gaussian estimator achieved a mean per-vertex reconstruction error of 3.717 mm for missing non-chamber structures, averaged over different observation patterns (1, 3, 5, 9 observed structures). The graph VAE obtained 5.248 mm error and nearest-neighbour retrieval 8.931 mm, yielding a paired improvement of 1.531 mm (95% CI 1.384–1.711) for the conditional estimator over the VAE, with consistent superiority also in a raw-coordinate sensitivity analysis. On 58 external CT cases with expert labels for five structures, the conditional estimator showed lower average surface distance, 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance, and Chamfer error for both completed atria. On another 20-case public benchmark, for which reference was adequate for three of four completed structures, the same performance ordering (conditional estimator best, then VAE, then nearest neighbour) was observed. Four modelled structures lack expert reference, so external quantitative validation for them is unavailable.
AI.conclusion: A carefully built multi-structure cardiac CT statistical shape model, when paired with its correct closed-form conditional Gaussian completion operator, can outperform more complex deep-learning approaches for cardiac shape completion, particularly for non-chamber structures. The released 11-structure model and estimator are suitable for research applications such as unifying heterogeneous CT cohorts in a shared anatomical space, but are not intended for direct clinical use. This work highlights the importance of proper probabilistic conditioning for completion tasks and provides a new, richly annotated shape resource to the community.

title: HealMed: Multilingual Evaluation of Large Language Models in Medicine
summary: We present HealMed, an expert-reviewed benchmark for multilingual evaluation of large language models in medicine. HealMed contains 1,000 examples in each of nine languages, drawn from nine datasets and covering three task formats: MCQA, NLI and open-ended QA. The benchmark was developed over two years by 23 physicians and medical experts based across nine countries and regions. Each translation was evaluated and revised by two experts fluent in English and the corresponding target language. On HealMed, performance declined most in low-resource languages, although the size of the gap varied markedly across languages and models. The strongest proprietary models were the most stable across languages, whereas many open-source and medically specialized models showed larger and less consistent gaps. Medical specialization alone did not ensure multilingual robustness. Furthermore, expert revision could either raise or lower measured performance, indicating that translation quality materially affects cross-language evaluation results.

AI.tldr: HealMed is a multilingual, expert-reviewed medical benchmark (9 languages, 1,000 items each, 3 task types) used to evaluate how robust large language models are across languages, showing notable performance drops in low-resource languages and highlighting the importance of translation quality.
AI.motivation: Existing medical LLM benchmarks are largely monolingual (often English-focused) and do not adequately test how well models perform in diverse languages and clinical contexts. This creates a gap in evaluating models for global, multilingual healthcare use. The authors aim to build a high-quality, expert-curated multilingual medical benchmark to systematically measure performance and robustness across languages, models, and task types.
AI.method: The authors created HealMed, a benchmark with 1,000 items per language in nine languages, drawn from nine underlying datasets and spanning three task formats: multiple-choice QA, natural language inference, and open-ended QA. Over two years, 23 physicians and medical experts from nine countries/regions curated, translated, and refined the items. Each translation from English into a target language was independently evaluated and revised by two bilingual medical experts to ensure clinical and linguistic correctness. They then evaluated a range of proprietary, open-source, and medically specialized LLMs on HealMed and compared performance across languages and model families.
AI.result: On HealMed, model performance decreased in lower-resource languages, but the size and pattern of the degradation varied substantially between languages and model types. Strong proprietary models showed relatively stable performance across languages, while many open-source and medically specialized models exhibited larger, more inconsistent performance gaps between languages. The study also found that applying expert revision to the translated items could either increase or decrease measured model performance, demonstrating that translation accuracy and nuance have a significant effect on cross-lingual evaluation outcomes.
AI.conclusion: HealMed provides a rigorous, expert-reviewed benchmark to assess multilingual medical capabilities of LLMs. The findings indicate that medical domain specialization by itself does not guarantee robustness across languages, and that multilingual evaluation must carefully consider translation quality, especially for low-resource languages. For reliable assessment and deployment of medical LLMs in global settings, both model design and benchmark construction need to explicitly account for linguistic diversity and the impact of translation processes.

title: Learning Early-to-Final Solution Consistency for MILP Acceleration
summary: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental problem class in operations research and combinatorial optimization, with broad applications to industrial decision-making. Owing to their NP-hardness, however, modern solvers may struggle to find high-quality solutions for challenging MILP instances within practical time limits. Recent learning-based approaches seek to accelerate MILP solving by directly predicting high-quality solutions from static instance-level features, such as variable-constraint bipartite graphs. Yet accurate solution prediction from instance features alone is difficult, and these methods largely overlook the information revealed during the solver's search process. In this paper, we find that solutions produced at the early search stage of MILP solvers, which are computationally cheap to obtain, are often structurally close to the solutions found after full-budget search. Motivated by this observation, we propose a new solver-informed paradigm that shifts the learning target from variable assignment to early-to-final consistency: for each variable, we predict whether its early-stage assignment should persist in full-budget solutions. The predicted consistency naturally guides downstream search, for instance by fixing the assignments deemed consistent. At inference time, we further ensemble consistency predictions across multiple early-stage solutions to improve robustness. Experiments across four MILP benchmarks show our method improves prediction-guided search across diverse downstream pipelines. With Gurobi, our proposed method reduces the primal gap by 56.9% on average and closes it completely on combinatorial auction instances. Besides, we transferred the Gurobi-trained model zero-shot to SCIP without adaptation, achieving a 36.4% average gap reduction across benchmarks.

AI.tldr: They use early-stage solutions from MILP solvers and learn to predict which early variable assignments will remain the same in the final high-quality solution, using these predictions to guide and speed up subsequent search.
AI.motivation: MILP solvers are powerful but can struggle to find high-quality solutions within practical time limits because MILP is NP-hard. Prior learning-based methods try to directly predict full solutions from static problem features, but this is difficult and ignores rich information produced during the solver’s search. The authors observe that early solutions are often structurally similar to final solutions, suggesting an opportunity to exploit this solver-generated information.
AI.method: Instead of predicting full variable assignments, they define a new learning target: for each variable, predict whether its assignment in an early-stage solution will be consistent with assignments in final, full-budget solutions. They train a model on solver-informed features to estimate this early-to-final consistency. At inference, they use the predicted consistent assignments to guide or partially fix variables in the subsequent search process. They further ensemble predictions over multiple early-stage solutions to improve robustness. The approach is integrated into existing MILP pipelines (e.g., Gurobi, SCIP) without altering the solvers’ core algorithms.
AI.result: On four MILP benchmark suites, their method consistently improves prediction-guided search. Using Gurobi, they achieve an average 56.9% reduction in primal gap and completely close the gap on combinatorial auction instances. The model trained with Gurobi transfers zero-shot to SCIP, still yielding an average 36.4% reduction in primal gap across benchmarks, demonstrating robustness and cross-solver generalization.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging early-stage solver solutions as informative signals and reframing learning as predicting early-to-final consistency is an effective paradigm for improving MILP solving. This solver-informed approach outperforms prior instance-feature-only methods, enhances multiple downstream search pipelines, and generalizes across different commercial solvers without retraining, suggesting a promising direction for combining optimization and learning.

title: Auditing Cross-Lingual Fairness in Language Model Watermarking
summary: Watermarking schemes for large language model output are evaluated almost exclusively on English text using each scheme's detection threshold and a narrow set of quality measurements. Multilingual deployment exposes evaluation-design choices that are inconsequential on English but determine conclusions cross-lingually. We propose an evaluation framework with four components: detection thresholds calibrated empirically per deployment context, a threshold-independent companion measurement that distinguishes calibration failures from detection failures, three disjoint quality measurement paradigms (distributional, paired-semantic, and reference-perplexity), and a generalized-entropy decomposition of cross-language disparity over a typological family partition. Applied to six watermarking schemes, three open-weight generators, eleven languages spanning four scripts and eight typological families, and both base and instruction-tuned regimes, the framework reveals failure modes that single-language single-paradigm evaluation cannot surface. Across detection and quality, observed disparity is predominantly between-family on the typological partition, indicating that cross-lingual fairness gaps in watermarking are structural to language properties rather than idiosyncratic to particular languages.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multilingual evaluation framework for watermarking schemes on large language model outputs, showing that current English-centric evaluations miss important cross-lingual failure modes and fairness gaps.
AI.motivation: Existing watermarking evaluations focus almost entirely on English, using scheme-specific detection thresholds and limited quality metrics. When watermarking is deployed in multiple languages, choices that seem benign in English (like fixed thresholds or narrow quality views) can significantly change conclusions about performance and fairness across languages. There is a need for a principled, language-aware evaluation framework that can expose where and why watermarking fails across diverse languages and typological families.
AI.method: The authors design an evaluation framework with four key components: (1) empirically calibrated detection thresholds tailored to each deployment context instead of relying on fixed or scheme-provided thresholds; (2) a threshold-independent companion metric that can distinguish whether poor performance is due to mis-calibration of the threshold or inherent detection limitations; (3) three distinct quality assessment paradigms—distributional metrics, paired semantic evaluations, and reference-based perplexity—to comprehensively measure the impact of watermarking on output quality; and (4) a generalized-entropy–based decomposition that partitions cross-language disparities into within-family and between-family components over a typological family grouping. They apply this framework to six watermarking methods, three open-weight LLM generators, 11 languages across four scripts and eight typological families, and both base and instruction-tuned model regimes.
AI.result: Using the framework, the authors uncover multiple failure modes in watermarking schemes that are not visible when evaluating only on English or with a single quality paradigm. They observe substantial cross-lingual disparities in both detection performance and quality impact. The generalized-entropy analysis shows that most of the disparity is between typological families rather than within them: languages in the same family behave more similarly, while different families exhibit systematically different detection and quality characteristics.
AI.conclusion: Single-language, single-metric evaluations of watermarking—especially those restricted to English—are insufficient and can be misleading about robustness and fairness in multilingual deployment. The proposed framework surfaces structural cross-lingual fairness gaps tied to linguistic typology, implying that watermarking design and evaluation must explicitly account for language properties. Effective, fair watermarking will require language-aware calibration, multi-paradigm quality assessment, and typology-informed analysis rather than assuming English performance generalizes cross-lingually.

title: Rethinking Patch Based Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Semantic Structured Partitioning
summary: Multivariate time series forecasting (MTSF) is a fundamental task in many real world applications. Existing patch based forecasting methods generally fall into three categories: fixed partitioning, multi-scale partitioning, and extendable partitioning. Fixed partitioning often breaks meaningful temporal boundaries, multi-scale partitioning may introduce redundant representations across scales, and extendable partitioning improves flexibility but still lacks an explicit mechanism for organizing semantic structure and modeling interactions among heterogeneous temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we propose SCPaT, a Transformer based framework built on semantic structured partitioning. SCPaT first decomposes input sequences into semantically consistent units through adaptive semantic unit generation, then constructs a dynamic semantic graph to model directed dependencies among these units and organize them into higher order semantic blocks. Based on these structured representations, an importance aware routing mechanism adaptively dispatches different semantic blocks to different experts for customized modeling. Extensive experiments on 12 real world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SCPaT.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SCPaT, a transformer-based framework that uses semantic structured partitioning and expert routing to improve multivariate time series forecasting.
AI.motivation: Existing patch-based multivariate time series forecasting methods—fixed, multi-scale, and extendable partitioning—either break meaningful temporal boundaries, create redundant representations, or lack explicit mechanisms to capture and organize heterogeneous temporal semantics and their interactions. There is a need for a method that adaptively discovers semantic units, structures them, and models their dependencies for better forecasting.
AI.method: SCPaT first performs adaptive semantic unit generation to decompose the input time series into semantically consistent units instead of rigid or scale-based patches. It then builds a dynamic semantic graph capturing directed dependencies among these units and groups them into higher-order semantic blocks. On top of these structured representations, an importance-aware routing mechanism sends different semantic blocks to different expert modules, enabling customized modeling per semantic type, all within a Transformer-based architecture.
AI.result: Across 12 real-world multivariate time series forecasting datasets, SCPaT achieves superior performance compared with existing patch-based and state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating better handling of heterogeneous temporal patterns and semantic structures.
AI.conclusion: Semantic structured partitioning combined with dynamic semantic graph modeling and importance-aware expert routing provides a more effective and flexible way to model multivariate time series for forecasting. SCPaT addresses the weaknesses of prior partitioning strategies by respecting semantic boundaries, reducing redundancy, and explicitly organizing and modeling interactions among heterogeneous temporal patterns.

title: SABET-QA: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
summary: Question Answering over Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGQA) requires reasoning over time-sensitive facts, yet existing embedding-based methods struggle with multi-step queries due to single-pass reasoning pipelines. We propose SABET-QA, a framework that iteratively refines reasoning states across multiple hops via a bidirectional entity-temporal scoring mechanism and a slot-aware contextualization module that aligns question semantics with temporal KG embeddings. A differentiable working memory enables progressive hypothesis refinement, while auxiliary temporal boundaries serve as coarse supervision when available. Experiments on CronQuestions, Complex-CronQuestions, MultiTQ, and TimeQuestions demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, particularly on complex multi-step temporal queries.

AI.tldr: SABET-QA is a new framework for temporal knowledge graph question answering that improves multi-step temporal reasoning through iterative refinement and temporal-aware alignment with questions.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal knowledge graph QA models, especially embedding-based ones, perform single-pass reasoning and thus struggle with complex, multi-hop, time-sensitive queries. There is a need for methods that can handle multi-step temporal reasoning more effectively.
AI.method: The paper proposes SABET-QA, which performs iterative, multi-hop reasoning by refining reasoning states over several steps. It introduces a bidirectional entity-temporal scoring mechanism and a slot-aware contextualization module to better align question semantics with temporal KG embeddings. It also uses a differentiable working memory to progressively refine hypotheses and optionally leverages auxiliary temporal boundaries as coarse supervision signals.
AI.result: Across several benchmarks—CronQuestions, Complex-CronQuestions, MultiTQ, and TimeQuestions—SABET-QA consistently outperforms strong baseline models, especially on complex multi-step temporal questions.
AI.conclusion: Iterative refinement with entity-temporal bidirectional scoring and slot-aware contextualization significantly enhances temporal KG question answering, particularly for complex multi-hop queries, demonstrating the effectiveness of SABET-QA for temporal reasoning tasks.

title: ReguSim: Evaluating LLM Agent Rule Grounding in Financial Compliance
summary: LLM agents in financial markets may cite rules yet still submit orders that violate executable constraints or misread surveillance evidence. We introduce ReguSim, a controlled financial-compliance environment, and ReguBench, a target-marked monitoring benchmark, to separate four artifacts: stated reasoning, attempted action, execution enforcement, and monitor evidence. In trader runs with DeepSeek V4 Pro and Gemini 3.5 Flash, visible rules reduce but do not eliminate rejected actions, and incentive or persona framing shifts behavior. A bridge study shows that trader rationales can mislead an independent monitor unless enforcement evidence is shown. In monitoring, simple structured baselines either match or exceed prompt-only LLMs. The results frame financial compliance evaluation as an audit of rule-grounded actions and evidence use, rather than a single compliance score.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ReguSim and ReguBench to study how LLM trading agents follow financial-compliance rules and how well monitors detect violations, showing that stated reasoning, actions, enforcement, and evidence must be evaluated separately.
AI.motivation: LLM agents deployed in financial markets may appear compliant in their explanations while still attempting non-compliant trades or misinterpreting surveillance signals. Existing evaluations often collapse reasoning, actions, and monitoring into a single metric, failing to capture how rules, incentives, personas, and enforcement evidence affect real behavior. There is a need for controlled environments and benchmarks that disentangle these components to rigorously study and improve financial compliance of LLM agents and LLM-based monitors.
AI.method: The authors build ReguSim, a controlled trading environment with explicit, executable regulatory rules and enforcement, and ReguBench, a benchmark for monitoring trader behavior with target-marked violations. They run LLM trading agents (e.g., DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.5 Flash) under different conditions: with or without visible rules, with varied incentive structures and persona framings. They log four artifacts for each episode: the model’s stated reasoning, the attempted trading actions, what is actually executed after enforcement, and the evidence presented to a monitor. They also conduct a bridge study where independent monitoring models assess trader compliance using either rationales alone or rationales plus enforcement evidence. Finally, they compare prompt-only LLM monitors against simple structured baselines on ReguBench.
AI.result: Visible rules in the trading environment decrease but do not fully prevent attempts to submit non-compliant orders; incentive and persona framing measurably shift model behavior. In the bridge study, trader-generated rationales can mislead independent monitoring LLMs into judging behavior as compliant unless concrete enforcement evidence is made available. On the monitoring side, simple structured methods (e.g., rule-based or feature-based baselines) achieve performance comparable to or better than prompt-engineered LLMs on ReguBench. Across all experiments, separating reasoning, actions, enforcement, and evidence reveals discrepancies that would be hidden in a single compliance score.
AI.conclusion: Financial-compliance evaluation for LLM agents should be framed as an audit process over multiple artifacts—rule-grounded reasoning, attempted and executed actions, and how evidence is used by monitors—rather than as a single aggregated compliance metric. ReguSim and ReguBench provide a principled way to study these dimensions, showing that visible rules, incentives, and personas affect behavior but do not guarantee compliance, and that monitoring systems must rely on concrete enforcement evidence instead of agent self-explanations. This multi-layered approach is necessary to design safer LLM traders and more reliable LLM-based surveillance tools in financial markets.

title: OenoBench: A Wine-Domain Benchmark for Knowledge-Grounded Evaluation of Large Language Models
summary: We introduce OenoBench, a wine-domain knowledge benchmark of 3,266 multiple-choice questions across six pillars (regions, grape varieties, viticulture, winemaking, producers, business) and four difficulty tiers. The corpus is built from 38,104 atomic, source-anchored facts extracted by 35 provenance-verified scrapers from government registries (INAO, TTB, OIV), peer-reviewed journals, and Wikipedia/Wikidata. Our methodological contribution is an LLM-driven pipeline in which language models reformat verified facts and audit the result, but never serve as the source of truth: every claim traces to a URL, every question is generated by one of five strategies across five generator families, and every question is scored by a nine-agent audit calibrated against a human gold sheet via Cohen's $κ$. Evaluating sixteen frontier configurations, we find: (i) overall accuracy spans 53%-84%, led by o3 at 83.6%; (ii) reasoning-mode lift concentrates in DeepSeek R1 (+6.8pp) and is absent in Claude Opus and Gemini Pro; (iii) Anthropic shows +9pp self preference on its own questions while Google shows -8pp inverse preference; (iv) frontier open-weight models share the cost-vs-accuracy Pareto frontier with proprietary reasoning models; and (v) every config gains around 33pp on closed-book solvable items, revealing a parametric-recall ceiling that only the contextual slice avoids. We release corpus, audit findings, human-review app, and construction code under CC-BY-SA-4.0.

AI.tldr: OenoBench is a large, source-grounded multiple-choice benchmark for wine-domain knowledge, built with an LLM-assisted but non-LLM-sourced pipeline and used to systematically evaluate frontier language models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks underrepresent specialized, structured, and professionally relevant domains such as wine, where knowledge spans regulations, geography, biology, and business.
