Many current benchmarks lack strong source grounding, fine-grained difficulty control, or careful auditing, making it hard to trust evaluations or to study reasoning vs recall. The authors want a high-quality, transparent, and domain-specific benchmark to stress-test LLMs on factual precision and reasoning in a complex but well-documented domain.
AI.method: They construct a corpus of 38k atomic facts scraped from authoritative wine-related sources (government registries, peer-reviewed journals, Wikipedia/Wikidata) using 35 provenance-verified scrapers. These facts are then transformed into 3,266 multiple-choice questions across six content pillars and four difficulty tiers using an LLM-based pipeline. In this pipeline, LLMs only reformat and generate question/answer structures from verified facts and audit the outputs; they are never used as original knowledge sources. Each question is associated with URLs for traceability and is generated using one of five strategies across five different LLM generator families to diversify style and content. Quality control is done via a nine-agent LLM audit whose judgments are calibrated to human gold labels with Cohen’s kappa to ensure reliability. They then evaluate sixteen frontier LLM configurations, including proprietary and open-weight, standard and reasoning-mode variants, on this benchmark.
AI.result: They observe substantial spread in performance, with overall accuracy ranging from 53% to 84%, and o3 achieving the highest accuracy at 83.6%. Reasoning modes do not universally help: DeepSeek R1 gains about +6.8 percentage points over its base, while Claude Opus and Gemini Pro show no reasoning-mode lift. Model providers show notable self- or inverse-preference effects on questions written by their own models, with Anthropic models performing about 9 percentage points better on Anthropic-generated questions and Google models about 8 points worse on Google-generated ones. Open-weight frontier models can match the cost–accuracy trade-offs of proprietary reasoning models, indicating competitiveness. All configurations gain roughly 33 percentage points on items solvable in a closed-book setting, suggesting a ceiling imposed by parametric recall that only questions requiring contextual information avoid.
AI.conclusion: OenoBench offers a rigorously grounded, transparent, and diversified benchmark for evaluating LLMs on specialized wine knowledge and related reasoning. The study shows that current frontier models vary widely in performance, that reasoning modes are not uniformly beneficial, and that provider-specific biases and parametric recall ceilings meaningfully shape results. By open-sourcing the corpus, audit artifacts, review tools, and construction code under CC-BY-SA-4.0, the authors aim to provide a reproducible platform for future research on domain-specific evaluation, model reasoning, and knowledge retrieval strategies.

title: Optimal Skill Selection for LLM Agents with Provable Bicriteria Guarantees
summary: Loading reusable skill documents into a bounded context window is now the primary way large language model (LLM) agents acquire task-specific capabilities, which makes skill selection a first-order determinant of task performance and token cost. Yet current agents score skills independently by semantic relevance and assemble the set by top-$k$ or greedy packing, with no quality guarantee or cost awareness on the selected set. As a result, redundant or poorly chosen skills waste scarce context tokens and can even degrade performance. We give the first model of how the selected skill set shapes execution outcomes and cast skill selection as an optimization problem: choose a skill set under a hard token budget to maximize a monotone submodular benefit minus context penalty. For this problem, we develop Best Prefix Selection (BPS), a polynomial-time algorithm, and prove, to our knowledge, the first performance guarantee for skill selection: a bicriteria $(1-1/e,1)$ approximation whose benefit coefficient is optimal in polynomial time. On a contamination-controlled BigCodeBench variant, BPS outperforms all the baselines, reaching $0.73$ measured task success versus $0.20$--$0.52$ for released skill routers, text retrievers, and the executor's own selection, on $28\%$ fewer tokens than the strongest released router.

AI.tldr: They propose and analyze a principled algorithm (BPS) for choosing which skill documents to load into an LLM’s limited context so as to maximize task performance per token.
AI.motivation: LLM agents rely on loading reusable skill documents into a limited context window to gain task-specific abilities. Current systems pick skills mainly by semantic relevance and simple top-k / greedy packing, which ignores token budgets, leads to redundant or low-quality selections, wastes context tokens, and can even harm performance. There is no formal model or guarantee for how the chosen skill set affects execution quality and cost, creating a need for an optimization-based, theoretically grounded selection method.
AI.method: They formalize skill selection as an optimization problem: under a hard token budget, choose a subset of skill documents that maximizes a monotone submodular benefit function minus a context penalty. Based on this formal model, they design Best Prefix Selection (BPS), a polynomial-time algorithm that selects skills with provable guarantees. They prove BPS achieves a bicriteria (1−1/e, 1) approximation, which is optimal for the benefit coefficient among polynomial-time algorithms. They then evaluate BPS empirically on a contamination-controlled variant of BigCodeBench against various baselines such as released skill routers, text retrievers, and the executor’s own selection strategy.
AI.result: BPS achieves a provable (1−1/e,1) bicriteria approximation for the submodular benefit-minus-penalty skill selection problem, with the benefit factor being provably optimal for polynomial-time algorithms. Experimentally on BigCodeBench, BPS substantially outperforms all evaluated baselines: it reaches 0.73 task success compared to 0.20–0.52 for existing skill routers, text retrievers, and the executor’s selection, and does so using 28% fewer tokens than the strongest released router.
AI.conclusion: A theoretically grounded optimization view of skill selection under token budgets leads to significantly better and more cost-efficient use of LLM context. The proposed BPS algorithm is the first with a formal performance guarantee for skill selection and shows strong empirical gains in task success and token efficiency over existing heuristic methods, indicating that principled subset selection is crucial for scalable, high-performance LLM agents.

title: When Text and Numbers Disagree: Evidence Arbitration in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in settings where textual summaries, numerical observations, and external tool outputs may provide conflicting evidence. We study how LLMs arbitrate between such sources when they support opposing decisions. To do so, we introduce a controlled synthetic benchmark in which latent risk trajectories generate both numerical time series and natural language summaries, allowing us to construct conflicts where exactly one evidence source is aligned with the ground-truth label. This design lets us independently manipulate modality, temporal recency, source reliability, and evidence provenance. Across open-weight instruction-tuned models, we find that arbitration behaviour is systematic rather than random: models exhibit distinct text-versus-number preferences, follow temporal recency more consistently than explicit reliability cues, and can over-rely on external forecasts even when they conflict with direct contextual evidence. These results suggest that current LLMs often rely on heuristic arbitration strategies when integrating heterogeneous evidence, highlighting a failure mode for tool-augmented decision systems.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how large language models reconcile conflicting textual, numerical, and tool-based evidence, revealing systematic but heuristic arbitration patterns that can cause failures in tool-augmented decision systems.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in decision-making scenarios that combine natural language reports, quantitative data, and external tool outputs, it is critical to understand how they choose between conflicting information sources. Mis-arbitration can lead to unreliable or unsafe decisions, yet this behavior is poorly characterized. The paper aims to systematically probe and quantify these arbitration behaviors under controlled conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct a synthetic benchmark where hidden (latent) risk trajectories generate both numerical time series and natural language summaries. They then design scenarios in which textual summaries, numerical data, and external tool forecasts can be put in conflict, with only one source matching the ground-truth label. By varying factors such as modality (text vs numbers), temporal recency of evidence, explicit reliability cues, and whether information comes from an external tool or direct context, they evaluate how different open-weight instruction-tuned LLMs arbitrate among these sources.
AI.result: The study finds that LLMs do not arbitrate randomly but follow systematic patterns. Models show distinct and model-specific preferences for text versus numerical evidence, tend to prioritize more recent information over explicitly stated reliability indicators, and often overweight external tool forecasts even when those forecasts contradict more reliable contextual evidence. These behavioral regularities are observed across multiple open-weight instruction-tuned models.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs rely on heuristic arbitration strategies when combining heterogeneous evidence sources, leading to predictable but potentially harmful failure modes in tool-augmented decision-making. The work implies that more principled mechanisms or training strategies are needed for robust evidence integration, particularly in safety-critical or high-stakes applications.

title: ExPhy: A Benchmark for Explicit Physical Property Learning in Multi-Object Trajectory Forecasting
summary: Understanding object dynamics requires not only predicting future trajectories but also examining whether a model captures the physical properties that govern motion. However, existing benchmarks rarely expose object-level physical properties as explicit evaluation targets alongside trajectory forecasting. To address this gap, we introduce \emph{ExPhy}, a multi-object trajectory forecasting benchmark containing 24,000 simulated physical scenes with explicit object-level labels for mass, friction, and restitution. ExPhy provides observed and future trajectories together with an in-distribution (ID) split and two out-of-distribution (OOD) splits over physical parameters (OOD-Parameter) and initial states (OOD-Initial) for jointly evaluating trajectory forecasting and physical property estimation. We further instantiate \textsc{PhyODE}, a physics-guided model with an explicit property interface that estimates physical properties from observed trajectories and uses them for differentiable future rollout. On the long-horizon OOD-Initial setting, \textsc{PhyODE} reduces ADE and FDE by 33.1\% and 31.0\%, respectively, compared with the strongest baseline. Zero-shot evaluation on ComPhy further assesses cross-benchmark transfer. Property-level analyses reveal that accurate trajectory forecasting does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of the underlying physical properties. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Zest86/ExPhy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ExPhy, a simulated multi-object trajectory forecasting benchmark with explicit physical property labels, and proposes PhyODE, a physics-guided model that jointly learns to estimate physical properties and forecast trajectories, showing strong OOD performance and revealing a disconnect between trajectory accuracy and property recovery.
AI.motivation: Most trajectory forecasting benchmarks only evaluate how well models predict object motion, without explicitly testing whether the models have captured underlying physical properties like mass, friction, and restitution. This makes it hard to assess physical understanding or generalization to new conditions. The authors aim to fill this evaluation gap by providing a benchmark where such physical properties are observable, and by studying models that explicitly infer and use them.
AI.method: They build ExPhy, a dataset of 24,000 simulated multi-object physical scenes with ground-truth object-level labels for mass, friction, and restitution. The dataset includes observed and future trajectories and is split into one in-distribution setting and two out-of-distribution splits: one where physical parameters differ (OOD-Parameter) and one where initial states differ (OOD-Initial). They also propose PhyODE, a physics-guided model with an explicit interface for physical properties: it first estimates physical properties from observed trajectories and then uses these inferred properties within a differentiable physics-inspired ODE-based rollout to forecast future trajectories. They compare PhyODE with baselines across ID and OOD splits and perform zero-shot transfer to another benchmark, ComPhy.
AI.result: On the challenging long-horizon OOD-Initial scenario, PhyODE significantly outperforms the strongest baseline, reducing Average Displacement Error (ADE) by 33.1% and Final Displacement Error (FDE) by 31.0%. The model also demonstrates some degree of cross-benchmark generalization under zero-shot evaluation on ComPhy. Detailed analyses at the property level show mismatches between trajectory forecasting accuracy and the accuracy of recovered physical properties.
AI.conclusion: ExPhy provides a new benchmark that explicitly couples trajectory forecasting with the estimation of key physical properties, enabling more rigorous evaluation of physical understanding in prediction models. PhyODE shows that explicitly modeling and using physical properties can substantially improve out-of-distribution, long-horizon trajectory prediction and support cross-benchmark transfer. However, the observed disconnect between good trajectory predictions and poor property estimation suggests that accurate motion forecasting alone is not sufficient evidence of true physical property understanding, motivating future work on models and training objectives that better align these aspects.

title: FormalTCS: Benchmarking End-to-End Frontier Formal Theoretical Computer Science Research of Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown growing potential for automated theoretical computer science (TCS) research, yet existing benchmarks remain far from realistic research settings. We introduce \ourbenchmark, an expert-validated benchmark for evaluating LLMs on frontier, end-to-end TCS research. \ourbenchmark contains $175$ instances drawn from papers accepted to STOC, FOCS, SODA, and COLT in 2025-2026, preserving paper-specific definitions, assumptions, and proof dependencies, with expert-verified Lean formalizations and proofs. Evaluations of leading LLMs reveal that current models remain far from reliably completing the full research pipeline. In particular, autoformalization is the sharpest bottleneck: the best model achieves only $11.5$ on translating natural-language claims into formal theorem statements, compared with $28.6$ Pass@8 when proving human-provided formal statements. Building on \ourbenchmark, we further develop an automated TCS research framework that generates, formalizes, filters, and proves new claims. Of $64$ generated claims, only $6$ ultimately pass expert evaluation and proof verification, indicating that beyond formalization, limited research taste remains another major barrier to autonomous TCS research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a realistic, expert-validated benchmark and framework for assessing and advancing LLMs in end-to-end theoretical computer science (TCS) research, revealing that autoformalization and research taste are major current bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks for mathematical and TCS reasoning are simplified and do not reflect the complexity, dependencies, and standards of real frontier research. The authors aim to create a benchmark that mirrors genuine TCS research workflows—capturing problem formulation, formalization, and proof—and to diagnose which stages most limit current LLMs. They also want to explore how far we are from autonomous TCS research, not only in proof search but also in generating meaningful, non-trivial new results.
AI.method: They construct \ourbenchmark, a benchmark of 175 instances sourced from accepted STOC/FOCS/SODA/COLT 2025–2026 papers. For each instance, they preserve the original paper’s specific definitions, assumptions, and proof dependencies, and provide expert-verified Lean formalizations and proofs. They then evaluate leading LLMs on subtasks in the TCS research pipeline, particularly (1) autoformalizing natural-language claims into formal theorem statements and (2) proving given formal statements. Beyond benchmarking, they build an automated research framework that uses LLMs (and Lean) to generate candidate new claims, autoformalize them, filter them, and attempt to prove them, with final human expert evaluation and proof verification of the surviving claims.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows a strong performance gap between autoformalization and proof search: the best LLM reaches only 11.5 (presumably percent or Pass@k) on translating natural-language claims into formal theorems, while achieving 28.6 Pass@8 when proving human-provided formal statements. In the end-to-end automated research framework, out of 64 LLM-generated candidate claims, only 6 pass both expert evaluation and formal proof verification, demonstrating low yield and highlighting that current systems rarely produce both interesting and correct TCS results without heavy curation.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are not yet capable of reliably executing frontier, end-to-end TCS research. Autoformalization is a more severe bottleneck than proof search, and even when formalization is overcome, the models’ “research taste” — their ability to propose non-trivial, valuable, and ultimately correct claims — is very limited. \ourbenchmark provides a rigorous, expert-validated testbed for measuring progress, and the authors’ automated framework exposes the key gaps that must be closed to achieve more autonomous TCS research systems.

title: Manifold Drift in Flow Preference Optimization: A Root Cause of Reward Hacking
summary: Preference optimization is a standard alignment method for generative models, yet extending it to continuous-time dynamics remains non-trivial. In flow matching, reward-driven updates modify transport trajectories without an inherent constraint to the pretrained data manifold and can move terminal samples off the pretrained support. We formalize this failure mode as manifold drift. Theoretically, we show that optimal flow matching recovers the terminal data distribution, whereas a preference update leaves the pretrained manifold whenever its induced terminal displacement has a nonzero normal component. As a remedy, we propose ThermoDPO, a temperature-controlled objective that anchors pairwise preference optimization on preferred samples. Across temperature regimes, this objective connects rejection sampling fine-tuning and FlowDPO and controls a pointwise reconstruction-based surrogate for manifold distance. To counteract diminished signals at low temperatures, we further introduce a weighted variant, ThermoDPO-weighted. On the main toy benchmark, ThermoDPO-weighted attains a StrictScore of 0.899, compared with 0.629 for FlowDPO and 0.857 for FlowDPO+RFT. On SD3.5-M at CFG = 4.5, it improves OCR by 47.5% and the average of four metrics by 16.0%.

AI.tldr: The paper studies preference optimization for continuous-time generative flows, identifies a failure mode called manifold drift where preference updates move samples off the pretrained data manifold, and proposes a temperature-controlled objective ThermoDPO (and a weighted variant) that anchors updates to preferred samples and significantly improves performance over FlowDPO on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Preference optimization effectively aligns discrete-time generative models (like language models) with human preferences, but extending it to continuous-time flow models is difficult. In flow matching, reward-driven preference updates can distort the transport trajectories so that terminal samples drift away from the pretrained data manifold, degrading sample quality. There is a need to formally understand this failure mode and to design a principled alignment method that preserves the data manifold while still incorporating preference signals.
AI.method: 1) The authors formalize manifold drift in the context of flow matching and theoretically analyze how standard preference updates can push terminal samples off the pretrained manifold whenever the terminal displacement has a nonzero normal component to the manifold. They prove that optimal flow matching itself recovers the correct terminal data distribution. 2) They introduce ThermoDPO, a temperature-controlled preference optimization objective for flows that anchors optimization around preferred samples, effectively interpolating between rejection sampling fine-tuning and FlowDPO as temperature varies. The objective controls a pointwise reconstruction-based surrogate for the distance to the data manifold. 3) To mitigate weak learning signals in the low-temperature regime (where updates become too conservative), they propose ThermoDPO-weighted, which re-weights samples or pairs to amplify informative preference signals. 4) They evaluate these methods on a toy benchmark (StrictScore metric) and on Stable Diffusion 3.5-M at specific classifier-free guidance (CFG) settings, measuring OCR and other quality metrics.
AI.result: On a toy benchmark, ThermoDPO-weighted achieves a StrictScore of 0.899, outperforming FlowDPO (0.629) and also FlowDPO with Rejection Fine-Tuning (FlowDPO+RFT, 0.857). On SD3.5-M at CFG = 4.5, ThermoDPO-weighted yields a 47.5% improvement in OCR performance and a 16.0% average improvement across four evaluation metrics relative to FlowDPO (or baseline methods), demonstrating better alignment without sacrificing sample quality due to manifold drift.
AI.conclusion: Preference optimization for continuous-time flow models suffers from a specific failure mode, manifold drift, where reward-based trajectory updates can move samples off the pretrained data manifold. By introducing ThermoDPO, a temperature-controlled alignment objective anchored on preferred samples, and its weighted extension to strengthen signals in low-temperature regimes, the authors provide a practical solution that both theoretically controls manifold distance and empirically yields substantial gains over existing flow preference optimization methods on toy and real-world benchmarks.

title: Task-CoEvolve: Efficient Harness Optimization via Adaptive Validation Task Selection
summary: We present a novel approach to efficient LLM agent harness optimization through adaptive validation task selection. Harness optimization iteratively rewrites the harness code based on validation performance, enabling substantial performance gains without updating the underlying model weights. Existing approaches, however, evaluate a fixed validation set in full at every iteration, incurring substantial evaluation costs even on tasks that become less discriminative as the harness evolves. We propose $\textbf{Task-CoEvolve}$, which co-evolves the validation tasks with the harness by addressing two challenges: selecting informative tasks and estimating full-set performance from partial evaluations. Task-CoEvolve builds on the observation that tasks on which candidate harnesses disagree are more informative for distinguishing among them than tasks that are consistently solved or failed. It uses variance-weighted sampling based on past outcomes to focus evaluation on tasks near the agent's capability frontier, with the sampling distribution adapting as the harness evolves. It then estimates full-set scores from the sampled tasks by accounting for their sampling probabilities, enabling consistent comparisons across iterations despite evaluating different subsets. Experiments on online text classification and Terminal-Bench 2.1 show that Task-CoEvolve consistently outperforms fixed-subset baselines and matches the final performance of full-set search while reducing the number of evaluations during optimization by 80%. Code will be released at https://github.com/Agent4Science-UTokyo/Task-CoEvolve.

AI.tldr: Task-CoEvolve adaptively selects and reweights validation tasks during LLM agent harness optimization, cutting evaluations by ~80% while matching full-validation performance.
AI.motivation: Harness optimization for LLM agents can significantly improve performance without retraining model weights, but current methods re-evaluate a large, fixed validation set every iteration. This is computationally expensive and wastes effort on tasks that are no longer informative once the harness improves or degrades. The authors aim to reduce evaluation cost while preserving or improving optimization quality by making validation more adaptive and information-efficient.
AI.method: They introduce Task-CoEvolve, which jointly evolves the choice of validation tasks and the harness code. First, they quantify task informativeness using disagreement among candidate harnesses: tasks near the agent’s capability frontier, where success is uncertain and outcomes vary, are more informative than tasks that are almost always solved or failed. They then perform variance-weighted sampling of tasks based on historical outcomes, emphasizing high-disagreement tasks. As optimization proceeds, the sampling distribution adapts to the changing harness capabilities. To ensure comparability across iterations despite evaluating only subsets, they estimate full-set performance from the sampled tasks via importance weighting that corrects for non-uniform sampling probabilities. This provides unbiased or consistent performance estimates while substantially reducing the number of task evaluations.
AI.result: On online text classification and Terminal-Bench 2.1 benchmarks, Task-CoEvolve yields better harness optimization than fixed-subset baselines and achieves essentially the same final performance as approaches that evaluate the full validation set every iteration. Crucially, it does so while reducing the number of validation evaluations during optimization by about 80%, demonstrating large computational savings with little or no loss in optimization effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, co-evolving validation task selection can make LLM agent harness optimization much more evaluation-efficient without sacrificing final performance. By focusing on tasks where candidate harnesses disagree and correcting for biased sampling when estimating full performance, Task-CoEvolve outperforms fixed-subset methods and matches full-set search at a fraction of the evaluation cost. This suggests that smarter validation strategies are a powerful lever for scaling practical LLM agent optimization.

title: Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combination
summary: Incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis has garnered significant attention in recent years. Existing approaches typically assume that data is missing at random or are designed specifically for certain missing patterns, ignoring the modality combination inconsistency between training and testing phases. However, in real-world scenarios, the testing phase often encounters modal combinations that were not present during the training phase, which leads to insufficient generalization capabilities and unstable performance. In this paper, we introduce the problem of Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combinations (IMSAUMC), aiming to enhance model generalization for unseen modality combinations. To address this challenge, we propose the model named $\textbf{C}$ontrastive $\textbf{M}$ixed $\textbf{P}$rompt $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textsf{CMPL}$) for IMSAUMC. It introduces a label-guided contrastive feature learning mechanism to learn robust and discriminative cross-modal representations. Additionally, we design modality-combination prompts with a soft router to facilitate better learning of various modality combinations. Furthermore, we introduce three prompt contrastive learning strategies, which enable effective learning of prompts corresponding to unseen modality combinations, thereby significantly strengthening the model's generalization capabilities in diverse testing scenarios. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets demonstrate that $\textsf{CMPL}$ achieves more than a 5% improvement in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses multimodal sentiment analysis when some modalities are missing and, importantly, when the test-time combinations of available modalities were never seen during training, proposing a contrastive mixed prompt learning framework that improves generalization to such unseen combinations.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal sentiment data (e.g., text, audio, video) often suffer from missing modalities, and the specific subsets of available modalities at test time may differ from those observed during training. Existing methods generally assume data is missing at random or are tailored to specific missing patterns, which fails to handle new modality combinations at inference and leads to poor generalization and unstable performance. There is a need for models that can robustly handle arbitrary and previously unseen modality combinations.
AI.method: The authors formalize a new problem setting: Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combinations (IMSAUMC). They propose CMPL (Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning), which has two key components: (1) a label-guided contrastive feature learning mechanism that encourages robust, discriminative cross-modal representations by pulling together samples with the same sentiment label and pushing apart different labels; and (2) modality-combination prompts routed via a soft router to represent different modality subsets. They further introduce three prompt contrastive learning strategies that train prompts so that the model can effectively infer and generalize to prompts corresponding to modality combinations that never appeared during training.
AI.result: On three standard multimodal sentiment datasets, CMPL outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by more than 5 percentage points in accuracy, indicating better robustness and generalization to incomplete and unseen modality combinations in testing scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that explicitly modeling unseen modality combinations via mixed prompts and contrastive learning substantially improves incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis. The CMPL framework generalizes better across diverse and previously unseen modality subsets, offering a more practical solution for real-world applications where missing modalities and new modality patterns are common.

title: Inject, Align, Recover: Staged Post-Training for Retrieval-Free Document Knowledge Internalization
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures. Includes Supplementary Material Sections A--G. Qian Kou and Xiaofeng Shi contributed equally and are co-corresponding authors. Hua Zhou is the project leader
summary: Large language models often fail to answer questions about a bounded document collection when the source documents are not retrieved at inference time. We study this setting as document knowledge internalization: converting a fixed corpus into usable parametric knowledge for retrieval-free question answering. We propose IAR (Inject, Align, and Recover), a three-stage post-training framework that separates structured document knowledge injection, QA behavior alignment, and general ability recovery. Unlike conventional continued pretraining, Inject converts source documents into continuation, rewrite, and instruction-conditioned reconstruction objectives. Align then adapts the injected model with answer-only QA supervision, while Recover merges the domain-adapted model with the base instruction model to recover general capabilities. Across Common Corpus (CC) and CCI, and across Llama, Phi, Qwen, and SmolLM model families, IAR improves the domain-primary domain-general frontier for retrieval-free document internalization. In the main comparison, IAR improves over Vanilla SFT on all four reported metrics in 7 of 8 dataset-model settings, with average gains of 3.6 percentage points in domain QA accuracy and 12.1 percentage points in mean general performance across IFEval, MMLU, and MSBench. Extended CC baselines show that LoRA and FAPM can win individual general metrics, but among methods that also reach leading or near-leading domain internalization, IAR retains one of the strongest general profiles.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes IAR, a three-stage post-training framework that more effectively “internalizes” a fixed document corpus into a large language model so it can answer domain questions without retrieval, while preserving general abilities.
AI.motivation: Large language models struggle to answer questions about a specific bounded document collection if the documents are not retrieved at inference time. Naive continued pretraining on the corpus often harms general capabilities and does not optimally transform corpus contents into parametric knowledge for question answering. The authors want a principled way to turn a fixed corpus into internal knowledge that supports retrieval-free QA, while retaining strong performance on broad, general benchmarks.
AI.method: They introduce IAR (Inject, Align, Recover), a three-stage post-training framework. Inject: convert source documents into a mix of training objectives—plain continuations, rewrites, and instruction-conditioned reconstructions—so that structured knowledge from the documents is embedded into the model. Align: fine-tune the injected model using answer-only QA supervision to shape its behavior for domain question answering. Recover: merge this domain-adapted model with the original base instruction-tuned model, in order to restore and preserve general capabilities while retaining the injected domain knowledge. They evaluate across two document corpora (Common Corpus, CC, and CCI) and multiple model families (Llama, Phi, Qwen, SmolLM), comparing against baselines including vanilla supervised fine-tuning, LoRA, and FAPM.
AI.result: Across CC and CCI and four model families, IAR consistently improves the trade-off between domain-specific QA performance and general abilities for retrieval-free document internalization. In head-to-head comparisons, IAR outperforms Vanilla SFT on all four metrics in 7 of 8 dataset-model combinations, with average gains of 3.6 percentage points in domain QA accuracy and 12.1 percentage points in mean general performance across IFEval, MMLU, and MSBench. Extended baselines show that while methods like LoRA and FAPM can achieve the best scores on some individual general benchmarks, when focusing on methods that also achieve strong domain internalization, IAR maintains one of the best overall general performance profiles.
AI.conclusion: IAR is an effective framework for turning a fixed document collection into parametric knowledge in LLMs, enabling retrieval-free domain QA while largely preserving or even improving general capabilities. By separating knowledge injection, QA behavior alignment, and capability recovery, it better navigates the domain–general trade-off than standard continued pretraining or simple SFT, and provides a strong baseline for future work on document knowledge internalization.

title: A three-dimensional typology of agency for advanced AI systems
summary: Research on the agency of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems focuses on agency as a normative concept and on the agency of particularly agentic AI systems. While recent work also focuses on the different profiles of agentic systems, no framework exists to address the question of the type of agency instantiated by advanced AI systems, particularly when considering non-moral forms of agency. Based on established theoretical positions in philosophy, ethics, legal theory and sociology, we develop a typology of agency for frontier AI systems consisting of three dimensions: the nature of agency (moral or legal), its mode (individual or collective) and its locus (human or non-human). Combining these dimensions produces eight possible instantiations of agency, which we classify as conventional, contested or controversial. The typology separates legal from moral agency and thereby creates conceptual space for considering individual, legal, non-human agency without presupposing that advanced AI systems are moral agents. We argue that this distinction is increasingly relevant where instrumental goal pursuit complicates the attribution of AI actions to particular human actors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured typology to classify different kinds of agency that frontier AI systems can possess, especially distinguishing moral from legal agency and human from non-human loci.
AI.motivation: Existing research on AI agency mostly treats agency as a normative concept and focuses on highly agentic systems, but lacks a clear framework to describe what *type* of agency AI systems instantiate, particularly for non-moral forms like legal or institutional agency. As advanced AI complicates responsibility attribution, there is a need for a conceptual tool that can systematically differentiate kinds of agency and clarify debates about AI as agents.
AI.method: The authors synthesize and extend established theoretical positions from philosophy, ethics, legal theory, and sociology to build a three-dimensional typology of agency. They define dimensions—nature (moral vs. legal), mode (individual vs. collective), and locus (human vs. non-human)—and then analyze the eight combinations these yield, categorizing each as conventional, contested, or controversial based on current theoretical and practical acceptance.
AI.result: They derive a matrix of eight possible agency types (e.g., individual moral human agency, collective legal human agency, individual legal non-human agency, etc.) and map each type to its status as conventional, contested, or controversial. This shows that some forms of AI agency—especially individual, legal, non-human agency—can be conceptualized without committing to AI moral agency, and highlights where current disagreements lie.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that separating legal from moral agency and systematically combining nature, mode, and locus of agency creates a clearer conceptual space for understanding and debating AI agency. This typology is particularly useful for cases where AI systems pursue instrumental goals in ways that obscure clear human responsibility, as it allows considering non-human legal agency while remaining neutral on whether AI are moral agents.

title: Inducing Task Models from Computer-Use Traces
summary: Naturalistic computer-use traces, passively recorded screenshots and mouse or keyboard actions, are a valuable resource for deriving symbolic, auditable, and reusable models of how everyday work is done. Such models matter as computer-use agents enter real work, where agents need to learn how tasks are actually performed, and organizations need to audit and reuse that knowledge. However, inducing such task models is challenging, as activity is observed only as low-level events and real-world work is multi-threaded with interleaved goals. Existing methods assume a given task or a single workflow, and produce step-level summaries rather than structured task models. We introduce Task Model Induction (TMI), which (i) discovers the latent tasks in an unconstrained trace, disentangling concurrent activity, and (ii) for each latent task, induces a task model pairing a hierarchical objective model of recursive goal decomposition with a procedure model of the control flow that organized the execution. Intrinsically, on controlled human and agent trajectories, TMI recovers interleaved tasks with 0.974 agreement against ground-truth groupings and reconstructs 74.9% of the observed execution steps, far more than the strongest workflow induction baseline. Extrinsically, skills derived from TMI's task models improve held-out task accuracy by 30.0% over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Task Model Induction (TMI), a method that automatically discovers and models interleaved tasks from naturalistic computer-use traces, producing hierarchical objective and procedural task models that outperform existing workflow induction methods.
AI.motivation: As computer-use agents increasingly support real-world work, there is a need for symbolic, auditable, and reusable models of how tasks are actually executed on computers. Naturalistic usage logs (screenshots, mouse/keyboard actions) contain this information but only as low-level, interleaved events. Existing methods assume a single known task or workflow and yield flat step summaries instead of structured task models capable of capturing concurrent, hierarchical, real-world activity. This gap limits agents’ ability to learn realistic task performance and organizations’ capacity to audit and reuse process knowledge.
AI.method: The authors introduce Task Model Induction (TMI), which analyzes unconstrained traces of computer activity to (1) automatically discover latent tasks and separate them from one another, even when their execution is interleaved, and (2) induce for each latent task a structured task model. Each task model combines a hierarchical objective model that captures recursive goal decomposition (how high-level goals break down into subgoals) with a procedure model that encodes the control flow organizing the execution steps. They evaluate TMI on controlled human and agent trajectories, comparing its recovered task groupings and execution-step reconstructions against ground-truth and baseline workflow induction methods, and also assess its impact on downstream task performance via skills derived from the induced models.
AI.result: On intrinsic evaluations using controlled traces, TMI recovers interleaved task groupings with 0.974 agreement with ground-truth and reconstructs 74.9% of the observed execution steps, substantially outperforming the best existing workflow induction baseline. On extrinsic evaluations, using the induced task models as skills, TMI yields a 30.0% improvement in held-out task accuracy over the strongest baseline, demonstrating both better interpretive fidelity to actual work and superior utility for downstream agents.
AI.conclusion: Task Model Induction (TMI) effectively transforms raw, naturalistic computer-use traces into structured, hierarchical task models that disentangle concurrent activities and capture both goals and control flow. It surpasses prior workflow induction approaches in accurately recovering task structure and execution details and provides practically useful skills that significantly boost performance on new tasks. This establishes TMI as a promising foundation for auditable, reusable models of real-world computer work and for training or augmenting computer-use agents operating in complex, multitasking environments.

title: On the Applicability of Safety Nets: A Safety-By-Design Solution for Certifying Neural Networks
summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in safety-critical aviation systems presents significant challenges for certification and deployment. Aviation, often regarded as the safest form of transportation, relies on numerous safety-critical systems. For future safety-critical AI-based systems, EASA requires a Safety-by-Design approach, which can be achieved by using Safety Nets that combine neural network compression with lookup tables to ensure 100 % correct runtime behavior across the discretized operational design domain. Although Safety Nets have been studied, no comprehensive study of their performance characteristics and system design trade-offs has been conducted. This work presents the first systematic analysis of the trade-off between neural network and lookup table size in Safety Nets. By systematically comparing neural networks with diverse architectures, this study identifies optimal design parameters that minimize overall storage and memory requirements while maintaining certification compliance. Results demonstrate that architectures with 3 to 5 hidden layers, each with approximately 50 to 100 nodes, combined with one-hot encoding, achieve the best balance. In these configurations, neural networks accurately represent at least 97 % of the data, while compact lookup tables handle the remaining errors. The resulting Safety Nets reduce the system size by almost three orders of magnitude, fitting within the memory budget of current avionics hardware while guaranteeing 100 % correct outputs across the entire discretized input space, as required by EASA guidelines. This work provides the first-ever open-source implementation of Safety Nets for HCAS and VCAS with replicable results, demonstrating a practical pathway toward certifiable AI-based systems in aviation and establishing Safety Nets as a viable Safety-by-Design solution for safety-critical applications.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes “Safety Nets,” a Safety-by-Design scheme that combines compressed neural networks with lookup tables to guarantee 100% correct behavior for AI in safety-critical aviation, optimizing architectures to fit current avionics hardware while meeting certification demands.
AI.motivation: AI promises benefits in aviation but is difficult to certify for safety-critical use because regulators (e.g., EASA) demand provable correctness over the entire operational design domain. Existing work proposed “Safety Nets” (NN + lookup table) but lacked a systematic study of how NN architecture and lookup table size trade off in terms of memory, storage, and certification constraints. The paper aims to fill this gap and make Safety Nets practically deployable.
AI.method: The authors systematically vary neural network architectures (depth, width, encoding schemes such as one-hot) within Safety Nets and measure how much of the discretized input space is correctly handled by the NN and how large the residual lookup table must be. They evaluate storage and memory requirements, targeting current avionics hardware, and identify configurations that satisfy a 100% correctness guarantee via the combined NN + lookup table while remaining certifiable under EASA’s Safety-by-Design expectations. They also implement and release open-source Safety Nets for concrete aviation collision-avoidance systems (HCAS and VCAS).
AI.result: Architectures with 3–5 hidden layers and roughly 50–100 nodes per layer, especially when using one-hot encoding, offer the best trade-off: the NN alone correctly represents at least 97% of the data, leaving only a small fraction of inputs to be covered by a compact lookup table. This configuration cuts total system size by nearly three orders of magnitude compared to naive tabular approaches, while still enabling 100% correct outputs over the discretized input space and fitting within existing avionics memory budgets.
AI.conclusion: Safety Nets—carefully designed combinations of compressed NNs and small lookup tables—can satisfy stringent aviation certification requirements by guaranteeing fully correct behavior over a discretized operational domain while remaining memory-efficient. With the first open-source implementations for HCAS and VCAS, the paper shows that AI-based safety-critical systems can be made certifiable and positions Safety Nets as a practical Safety-by-Design paradigm for aviation and potentially other safety-critical domains.

title: G-CARL: Grounded Checklist-Aligned Reward Learning for Patient-Oriented Medical Report Interpretation
summary: Personalized interpretation of medical reports has emerged as an increasingly important need among patients. Addressing this need requires both evidence-grounded medical factuality and context-dependent patient communication, yet existing medical vision-language tasks do not adequately capture these dual requirements. To bridge this gap, we introduce Patient-oriented Medical Report Interpretation (PMRI), a novel open-ended multimodal generation task that requires models to explain medical reports in accurate and accessible language based on a user's query and dialogue history. These two objectives differ fundamentally in their verifiability, yet remain tightly coupled, making them difficult to optimize jointly under conventional supervised fine-tuning and holistic reinforcement learning paradigms. To address this challenge, we propose G-CARL, a grounded, checklist-aligned reinforcement learning framework that combines multi-source retrieval for atomic claim verification with context-aware, instance-specific weighted checklists for response coverage, providing structured supervision for factuality, user-demand satisfaction, and expression quality without constraining response diversity. We further construct MMedReport, a real-world PMRI benchmark, along with a clinician-designed three-dimensional evaluation protocol. Extensive experiments demonstrate that G-CARL consistently outperforms existing post-training baselines in overall quality, claim-level precision, and checklist recall. Pairwise preference evaluation by clinicians further confirms that G-CARL produces interpretations that are more accurate and better aligned with patient needs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PMRI, a new task and dataset for patient-oriented explanations of medical reports, and proposes G-CARL, a reinforcement learning framework that improves factual, patient-centered medical report interpretations.
AI.motivation: Patients increasingly need personalized, understandable explanations of their medical reports. Existing medical vision-language tasks mainly focus on factual description or generic reporting and do not jointly capture two critical needs: (1) strict medical factuality grounded in evidence, and (2) tailored, context-aware communication that addresses a specific patient’s questions and dialogue history. Moreover, these two objectives—factual correctness and patient-oriented communication—are fundamentally different in how they can be verified, yet closely intertwined in practice, making it hard to optimize them together with standard supervised fine-tuning or holistic RL approaches.
AI.method: The authors define a new task called Patient-oriented Medical Report Interpretation (PMRI), which is an open-ended multimodal generation task where models must explain medical reports based on a user query and prior dialogue. To optimize models for this task, they propose G-CARL, a grounded, checklist-aligned reinforcement learning framework. G-CARL uses multi-source retrieval to verify atomic factual claims in model outputs and employs context-aware, instance-specific weighted checklists to evaluate coverage of user needs. These checklists encode desired aspects such as factuality, satisfaction of user demands, and expression quality. The RL signal is thus decomposed and structured instead of being a single holistic reward, guiding generation without restricting response diversity. They also construct MMedReport, a benchmark dataset for PMRI, and design a clinician-informed three-dimensional evaluation protocol.
AI.result: Experimental results show that models trained with G-CARL outperform various post-training baselines on the MMedReport benchmark. The improvements are observed in overall output quality, precision at the level of individual factual claims, and recall with respect to the checklist items (i.e., how well the responses cover the required aspects). Additionally, clinicians perform pairwise preference evaluations and more frequently prefer the outputs generated by G-CARL-trained models, judging them to be both more factually accurate and better aligned with patient needs compared to baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that PMRI fills an important gap by explicitly targeting patient-oriented explanation of medical reports and that G-CARL is an effective framework for optimizing models on this task. By combining grounded claim verification with checklist-aligned rewards, G-CARL can enhance medical factuality, coverage of patient information needs, and communication quality simultaneously, without sacrificing generative flexibility. The new MMedReport benchmark and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for future work on safe, patient-centered medical report interpretation systems.

title: What You Can't See Is What You Learn: Restricted Evidence Visibility Favors Compositional Generalization in Shared-Genome Language-Model Societies
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Code and evaluation records: https://github.com/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning ; checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/tokenosopher/populus-evidence-partitioning-checkpoints
summary: Multi-module systems often expose every module to the full input. We test whether restricting evidence visibility changes which solutions gradient-based training discovers. Four-cell societies share one frozen pretrained language model and one low-rank adapter, communicating only through two model-width continuous vectors in a fixed relay. On a prospectively sealed natural-language function-composition task, we train ten matched restricted/global pairs sharing initialization bytes, training order, token layout, parameters, and computation; only the attention mask differs. Restricted societies outperform their globally visible twins by at least 20 points at both depths in 9 of 10 pairs, with median paired advantages of 0.7648 and 0.6050. Cutting communication reduces every restricted society to chance, and the depth-three advantage remains 0.558 on programs whose composite function never appeared in training. Across six audited restricted societies, same-value packet transplants preserve behavior at 0.94-1.00 across all tested interfaces; destructive interventions collapse performance; and counterfactual packets redirect outputs toward the mathematically predicted answer. The sole high-performing global model also requires communication, but its same-value packets are not interchangeable across episodes. Restricted visibility is thus not necessary for composition; under this protocol it substantially increases the probability of a generalizing relay and favors a reusable, value-indexed interface. The complete preregistered battery nevertheless formally fails because restricted-arm median depth-three accuracy is 0.6988, below the 0.70 floor. An earlier qualification cohort likewise yielded 0/10 complete passes: one model met every task-performance gate, but all ten failed ordinary-language preservation, confining the system to explicitly task-gated use.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how restricting information visibility between modules of a language-model-based system affects the solutions found by gradient-based training, finding that restricted communication architectures tend to generalize compositionally better than fully global ones.
AI.motivation: In many multi-module or multi-agent systems using neural networks, each module has access to the full input through global attention. It is unclear whether this global visibility helps or hinders the emergence of compositional solutions that generalize systematically, especially on tasks requiring function composition. The authors aim to test whether limiting what evidence each module can see, and forcing them to communicate through narrow, structured channels, changes which solutions training discovers and whether it improves generalization and interpretability.
AI.method: The authors build "four-cell societies" composed of a shared frozen pretrained language model and a shared low-rank adapter. The cells communicate only through two model-width continuous vectors passed along a fixed relay, with the only experimental manipulation being the attention mask: restricted-visibility vs fully global visibility. They evaluate these systems on a prospectively sealed natural-language function-composition task, training ten matched pairs of restricted vs global models with identical initialization, training order, token layouts, parameters, and compute. They then ablate and intervene on communication channels, transplant packets, and perform counterfactual manipulations to probe whether representations are reusable and value-indexed, and whether performance depends on communication. They also audit generalization to composite functions never seen during training and report on preregistered performance thresholds across cohorts.
AI.result: Restricted-visibility societies outperform their global-visibility twins by at least 20 percentage points at both tested depths in 9 out of 10 matched pairs, with median performance advantages of about 0.76 and 0.61, respectively. Disabling communication channels drops restricted systems to chance, indicating reliance on the relay; yet depth-three performance advantage persists (0.558) even on unseen composite functions, suggesting genuine compositional generalization. In six audited restricted systems, swapping same-value packets across interfaces preserves behavior almost perfectly (0.94–1.00), destructive interventions destroy performance, and counterfactual packets steer outputs toward mathematically predicted answers. The only strong global model also requires communication but lacks interchangeable same-value packets. Despite these strong qualitative results, the preregistered battery is formally failed because median depth-three accuracy for the restricted arm is 0.6988, below the 0.70 cutoff, and an earlier qualification cohort also had 0/10 complete passes due to failures in ordinary-language preservation.
AI.conclusion: Restricting visibility between modules is not strictly necessary for function composition, but under the studied protocol it significantly increases the likelihood that training discovers a generalizing, relay-based solution with reusable and value-indexed internal interfaces. Structured, narrow communication encourages the emergence of interpretable and transplantable internal representations, while fully global attention tends to produce solutions that are less modular and less systematically compositional. However, strict preregistered performance thresholds were not met, so the formal experimental battery technically fails, underscoring both the promise and the remaining limitations of the approach.

title: ConceptGuard: Benchmarking Context-Sensitive Unlearning in Large Language Models
comment: Submitted to NeurIPS E&D Track 2026; 17 pages, 9 figures
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly require selective removal of harmful or sensitive knowledge, called unlearning, yet existing methods and benchmarks fail to evaluate this capability completely. Current approaches rely on disjoint forget and retain sets composed of independent facts, and measure success using simple and direct factual recall. This framing fails to capture a key requirement of unlearning, namely the ability to eliminate harmful behaviors while preserving benign and beneficial knowledge. We argue that effective unlearning must operate at the level of concepts, ensuring complete removal of unsafe applications while maintaining their correct and useful usage, thereby achieving conceptually meaningful and complete unlearning. To better evaluate unlearning techniques from such a practical viewpoint, we introduce the notion of dual-use concepts: concepts that can be used in both harmful and benign contexts. Building on these concepts, we construct a benchmark called ConceptGuard where forget and retain sets are explicitly complementary in concept usage. Our benchmark uniquely enables unlearning to be explored and gauged at the level of concepts, instead of sparse facts, and evaluation is intent-sensitive with the goal of maximizing contextual separation to promote safer behavior. We demonstrate that current unlearning techniques perform poorly under this setting, showing weak contextual separation alongside poor performance in ROUGE and concept-level metrics. Our results reveal strong forgetting-utility trade-offs, limited gains in contextual sensitivity, and poor consistency in concept-level control across methods, and provide ideas for unlearning approaches that better align with real-world safety requirements. Our dataset is publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ConceptGuard, a benchmark to evaluate LLM unlearning at the level of dual-use concepts, showing that current unlearning methods struggle to remove harmful uses while preserving benign ones.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM unlearning methods and benchmarks focus on isolated facts and simple recall, which does not reflect the real-world need to remove harmful behaviors while preserving useful capabilities, especially for dual-use knowledge. There is a need for an evaluation framework that captures intent-sensitive, concept-level unlearning to better align with safety requirements.
AI.method: The authors define dual-use concepts—knowledge that can be applied in both harmful and benign ways—and then construct a benchmark, ConceptGuard, where forget and retain sets are complementary in terms of concept usage rather than disjoint facts. They design evaluations that are intent-sensitive and emphasize contextual separation between harmful and benign applications. They then test existing unlearning methods on this benchmark using ROUGE and concept-level metrics to assess contextual sensitivity, forgetting-utility trade-offs, and consistency of concept control.
AI.result: When evaluated on ConceptGuard, existing unlearning techniques perform poorly: they show weak contextual separation between harmful and benign uses, suffer from strong trade-offs between forgetting harmful uses and retaining utility, and achieve low scores on ROUGE and concept-level metrics. Additionally, they show inconsistent control at the concept level across different methods.
AI.conclusion: Concept-level, intent-sensitive unlearning is substantially harder than what current benchmarks suggest, and present unlearning methods are inadequate for dual-use concepts. ConceptGuard provides a more realistic and stringent benchmark that reveals forgetting-utility trade-offs and gaps in contextual sensitivity, highlighting the need for new unlearning approaches that can achieve complete and meaningful concept-level unlearning while maintaining beneficial uses in real-world safety scenarios.

title: DECOWAM: Decoupled Whole-Body World-Action Model for Legged Mobile Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Introduces DECOWAM, a decoupled whole-body world-action model for legged mobile manipulation, and the ARMDOG real-robot dataset
summary: Mobile manipulation requires a robot to predict how locomotion and arm motion jointly alter future observations and control. Existing world-action models, developed largely for fixed-base platforms, do not explicitly distinguish camera ego-motion from base and arm actions. Here we introduce DECOWAM, a whole-body world-action model that separates these factors through dedicated conditional interfaces. DECOWAM freezes an adapted FastWAM backbone and trains residual adapters, an action-equivalent future bottleneck distilled from privileged observations, adversarially separated base and arm latents, and base-velocity conditioning for video prediction. We further introduce ARMDOG, a real-robot dataset that synchronizes video, whole-body state and action, and language. On a fixed replay protocol, DECOWAM improved both future-video and action prediction over FastWAM, reducing action MSE by 21.7% with 25.95M trainable adaptation parameters. Across 79 closed-loop trials per method, it achieved the highest observed whole-body coordination and base-displacement robustness among the compared systems, while task completion remained comparable to the strongest baseline. These results show that embodiment-aware factorization can support parameter-efficient joint visual prediction and whole-body control under moving viewpoints.

AI.tldr: They propose DECOWAM, a world-action model for mobile manipulation that explicitly factors camera ego-motion, base, and arm actions, and show it improves prediction and control with few extra parameters, using a new ARMDOG dataset.
AI.motivation: Prior world-action models, mainly designed for fixed-base robots, do not explicitly separate visual changes caused by the robot’s camera motion from those caused by base and arm actions. For mobile manipulators, where whole-body coordination and moving viewpoints are critical, this entanglement hinders accurate future video and action prediction and robust control. The paper aims to build an embodiment-aware model that better captures how locomotion and arm motion jointly affect observations and control.
AI.method: They introduce DECOWAM, a whole-body world-action model with explicit factorization of camera ego-motion, base, and arm influences via dedicated conditional interfaces. Technically, they: (1) adapt and then freeze a FastWAM backbone; (2) train lightweight residual adapters on top; (3) use an action-equivalent future bottleneck distilled from privileged observations; (4) adversarially separate base and arm latent representations; and (5) condition video prediction on base velocity. They also provide ARMDOG, a real-robot dataset with synchronized video, full-body state/action, and language annotations, and evaluate under a fixed replay and closed-loop control protocol.
AI.result: On a fixed replay protocol, DECOWAM improves both future video and action prediction over the FastWAM baseline, cutting action MSE by 21.7% using only 25.95M trainable adaptation parameters. In 79 closed-loop trials per method, DECOWAM shows the best whole-body coordination and robustness to base displacement among compared systems, while maintaining task completion rates on par with the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling embodiment by factorizing camera, base, and arm effects enables more parameter-efficient joint visual prediction and whole-body control for mobile manipulators under moving viewpoints. DECOWAM’s design and the ARMDOG dataset demonstrate that separating base and arm latents and conditioning on base motion can significantly enhance action and video prediction as well as closed-loop coordination, without sacrificing task performance.

title: DARS: Dual-Level Credit Assignment RL with Structured Reasoning for Instruction-Based Image Editing
summary: Instruction-based image editing uses a planner-renderer pipeline: a vision-language model (VLM) first converts the instruction into an edit plan, and a diffusion model then executes that plan. Training such systems with only final-image rewards is inefficient because a poor edit does not reveal whether additional optimization should place more emphasis on the planner or the renderer, and even planner-dominant cases remain difficult to localize within a free-form reasoning trace. We present DARS, a reinforcement learning framework for dual-level credit assignment in this two-stage setting. Across modules, multi-plan multi-render rollouts estimate between-plan and within-plan reward variability for soft module routing, while rollout mean rewards provide hardness estimates for an adaptive curriculum. Within the planner, a four-field structured reasoning output enables a prefix-gated reward and token-level advantage reweighting, turning outcome-level feedback into localized supervision. Experiments on five benchmarks show that DARS outperforms a Joint~RL baseline with the same backbone, data, reward model, and rollout budget, with the largest gains on reasoning-intensive edits.

AI.tldr: DARS is a reinforcement learning framework that improves instruction-based image editing by assigning credit at both the planner and renderer levels using structured rollouts and token-level reasoning supervision.
AI.motivation: Existing instruction-based image editing systems use a planner (VLM) and a renderer (diffusion model), but training them with only final-image rewards is inefficient. When the final edit is poor, it is unclear whether the planner or the renderer is at fault, and planner errors are hard to localize within free-form reasoning traces. This leads to slow and suboptimal learning.
AI.method: DARS introduces dual-level credit assignment. Across modules, it performs multi-plan multi-render rollouts to estimate reward variability between and within plans, enabling soft routing of learning signal to either planner or renderer, and uses mean rollout rewards to compute hardness estimates for an adaptive curriculum. Within the planner, it enforces a four-field structured reasoning output; this structure allows prefix-gated rewards and token-level advantage reweighting so that outcome-level rewards are converted into localized supervision on specific parts of the planner’s reasoning trace.
AI.result: On five image-editing benchmarks, DARS is empirically compared with a Joint RL baseline that uses the same backbones, data, reward model, and rollout budget. DARS consistently outperforms this baseline, with especially large improvements on tasks that demand complex reasoning in the planning stage.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling and exploiting reward variability across plans and within the planner’s reasoning trace, DARS provides effective dual-level credit assignment in planner-renderer pipelines. This leads to more efficient and stronger learning for instruction-based image editing, especially on reasoning-intensive edits, without changing the underlying architectures or supervision sources.

title: The Third Restructuring of Software Form: From the Three-Tier Architecture to Storage, Models, and Agents
summary: Software form has undergone two paradigm shifts since its inception: Software 1.0, in which instructions determine behavior, and Software 2.0, in which data determines behavior (machine learning). This paper argues that a third shift - Software 3.0, in which context and reasoning determine behavior - is now underway, and contends that its terminal form converges to three elements: a generalized database (the unified abstraction of all persistent state and memory), a large model (the intelligence core that performs reasoning and generation), and an agent (the execution loop connecting the first two). The core argument is as follows: in the traditional three-tier architecture, the user-interface layer will be absorbed by the model's ability to generate interfaces on demand, the business-logic layer will be re-partitioned along "expressibility x criticality" into model reasoning and storage constraints (with residual deterministic logic retained as tools), and only the data layer will be elevated into the sole persistent infrastructure. We formalize this convergence thesis, present a minimal reference architecture, report evidence from real prototypes and a live model, and systematically analyze both the conditions under which it holds and the boundaries where it fails - determinism, cost, security, and verifiability delimit the thesis's domain of applicability. We argue that the thesis holds in task domains that are expressible, verifiable, externally stateful, and tool-complete, and that it will reshape the roles of developers, the database industry, and the software-engineering discipline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes 'Software 3.0', a new paradigm where context and reasoning, powered by large models and unified data, drive software behavior.
AI.motivation: Current paradigms (Software 1.0: explicit code; Software 2.0: data-driven ML) cannot fully exploit modern foundation models, contextual reasoning, and agents. There is a need to rethink software architecture to align with emerging capabilities of large models and agentic systems and to understand how this will transform software engineering, databases, and developer roles.
AI.method: The authors conceptually analyze existing three-tier architectures and show how each layer is transformed in Software 3.0. They define a convergence thesis centered on three elements (generalized database, large model, agent), formalize this as a reference architecture, and evaluate it using real prototypes and a live model. They then delineate the domain of applicability by analyzing constraints like determinism, cost, security, and verifiability.
AI.result: They derive a minimal reference architecture for Software 3.0 composed of a generalized database, a large reasoning/generative model, and an agentic execution loop. They show empirical evidence from prototypes and a live deployment that many UI, business-logic, and workflow concerns can be subsumed by model-driven reasoning plus data, with deterministic tools handling the remaining critical logic.
AI.conclusion: Software is entering a third paradigm in which context and reasoning, implemented via large models operating over unified data and orchestrated by agents, become the primary drivers of behavior. This Software 3.0 architecture applies to domains that are expressible, verifiable, externally stateful, and tool-complete, and it will significantly reshape how developers work, how databases are designed and used, and how software engineering as a discipline conceptualizes systems.

title: MemTrapBench: Benchmarking Cognitive Traps in LLM Memory Use
summary: Memory has become a key component of large language models, enabling them to retain information and learn from long-term interactions. However, existing memory benchmarks mainly evaluate whether information is correctly extracted, stored, and retrieved, while largely overlooking how retrieved memories reshape model reasoning and affect performance on the current task. We identify memory-induced cognitive traps: even faithfully recorded and semantically relevant memories can distort model reasoning or beliefs and degrade current task performance. To systematically evaluate these failure modes, we introduce MemTrapBench, which covers two forms of cognitive traps: Reasoning Fixation and Belief Distortion. Experiments across two model families and five representative memory frameworks show that MemTrapBench is challenging: all evaluated memory strategies underperform the no-memory setting, with even the strongest methods suffering drops of more than 10%. To mitigate these cognitive traps, we propose AdaptiveMem, a simple yet effective inference-time method that instructs LLMs to avoid memory traps. AdaptiveMem mitigates cognitive traps on MemTrapBench while preserving or improving performance on standard memory benchmarks across diverse memory frameworks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MemTrapBench, a benchmark revealing that LLM memories can hurt current-task reasoning via cognitive traps, and proposes AdaptiveMem, an inference-time strategy that reduces these traps while maintaining or improving standard memory performance.
AI.motivation: Current memory benchmarks for LLMs focus on whether models can correctly extract, store, and retrieve information, but largely ignore how retrieved memories influence ongoing reasoning and task performance. The authors observe that even accurate and relevant memories can bias or derail reasoning, a failure mode that is underexplored yet critical for safe and effective long-term interaction. They aim to systematically characterize and measure these memory-induced cognitive traps, and to find ways to mitigate them.
AI.method: The authors first conceptualize and define memory-induced cognitive traps in LLMs, focusing on two main categories: Reasoning Fixation (over-focusing on remembered patterns or solutions) and Belief Distortion (miscalibrated or shifted beliefs due to prior memories). They then design MemTrapBench, a benchmark composed of tasks that intentionally provoke these traps, and evaluate multiple memory frameworks and LLM families under this benchmark, comparing them to a no-memory baseline. To address the problem, they propose AdaptiveMem, an inference-time prompting/control strategy that explicitly instructs the model to be cautious about memory use and to avoid falling into the identified traps. They test AdaptiveMem across models and memory frameworks on both MemTrapBench and standard memory benchmarks.
AI.result: Across two LLM families and five representative memory frameworks, all tested memory strategies perform worse on MemTrapBench than a no-memory baseline, with even the best methods losing more than 10% in performance, demonstrating the severity of cognitive traps. When applying AdaptiveMem, the models show reduced vulnerability to these traps on MemTrapBench. At the same time, AdaptiveMem maintains or improves performance on existing standard memory benchmarks across different memory setups, indicating that it mitigates harmful memory effects without sacrificing normal memory benefits.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that adding memory to LLMs can systematically harm current-task reasoning via cognitive traps, even when memories are accurate and relevant, highlighting a blind spot in existing evaluation. MemTrapBench provides a structured way to evaluate these issues, and the proposed AdaptiveMem inference-time method effectively mitigates such traps while preserving or enhancing conventional memory performance. The authors conclude that robust LLM memory systems must be evaluated not only on retrieval accuracy but also on their impact on reasoning, and that explicit mechanisms for cautious, adaptive use of memory are necessary.

title: ContractScrub: A benchmark for final review of legal contracts
summary: Legal work, with its heavy reliance on processing large amounts of text, is often considered one of the domains most exposed to the use of LLMs. Contract ``scrubbing,'' the final review of transactional agreements for errors and inconsistencies, is a particularly suitable task for automation, because it is routine, painstaking work requiring detailed attention to long documents. Scrubbing also seems to align naturally with the general capabilities expected of frontier LLMs around long-context reasoning, consistency checking, and named entity recognition (NER). Despite the economic value and potential for automation, no formal evaluations of LLMs performing contract scrubbing have been conducted. We introduce ContractScrub, the first benchmark designed to evaluate contract scrubbing capabilities, comprising contracts hand-crafted by experienced lawyers over diverse error categories such as misuse of defined terms, incorrect references, and inconsistent language. Frontier models perform surprisingly poorly with only one model reaching 0.75 macro average recall despite strong performance on seemingly related general benchmarks, demonstrating the practical limits of current models and the importance of narrowly targeted, domain-specific benchmarks for measuring real-world impact.
